title: review-cli --detach/jobs: job-id validation ordering, signal-reaper spawn race, shared-/tmp symlink hardening, cross-process job discovery
body:
## What
Two rounds of `review diff --staged` (dogfooding the #162 log-fallback fix) surfaced several deeper issues in the `--detach`/job-tracking feature (review-cli#160) that are out of scope for #162 itself (the sandboxed log/jobs-dir write fix) but are real and should be tracked:

1. **Job-id validation happens after the lock file is opened.** `write_job()` calls `_job_lock()` (which opens `<jobs_dir>/<job_id>.lock`) before `job_path()` validates the id shape. A crafted `$REVIEW_JOB_ID` (e.g. an absolute path or `../` traversal) can create a `.lock` file OUTSIDE `jobs_dir()` before `InvalidJobId` is ever raised. Fix: validate the id at the very start of `write_job()` (and in `_job_lock_path()` itself), before any filesystem call.

2. **Signal-reaper spawn race.** `install_signal_reaper()`'s handler calls `kill_live_children()`, but a signal delivered between `Popen()` and `_register_child()` still leaves that one backend child unregistered and un-reaped — the existing tests manually pre-register a child before signaling, so they can't catch this window. Needs a handshake (or making spawn+register atomic from the handler's perspective) plus a test that signals during a real, in-flight `_run_streamed` registration.

3. **Shared-/tmp fallback directories aren't hardened against a symlink/pre-creation attack.** `_fallback_log_dir()` and `jobs_dir()`'s temp-dir fallback use a PREDICTABLE path (`/tmp/review-cli-{logs,jobs}-<uid>`). On a shared multi-user box, another user could pre-create that path (or a symlink at that path) before this process does, potentially redirecting secret-bearing logs/job argv elsewhere. Needs an `lstat`-based ownership/type check (reject a non-owned directory or a symlink) before trusting the path, or use `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` semantics throughout.

4. **Cross-process job discovery breaks once the temp-dir fallback's `mkdtemp()` tier is hit.** `jobs_dir()`'s last-resort tier is memoized only within the process that first hits it; `$REVIEW_JOBS_DIR` is propagated from a `--detach` spawn to ITS child, but a LATER, unrelated `review status <job-id>` invocation (a fresh process, no inherited env) has no way to find that same directory and will report "no such job". Needs either a stable, discoverable last-resort location (not a fresh `mkdtemp()` each cold process) or a documented/recorded pointer file at a well-known path.

## Why (motivation)
These are real correctness/security gaps in the `--detach`/job-tracking feature, found via AI code review while fixing an unrelated but adjacent bug (#162). Tracking them separately keeps #162 (log-fallback fix, which several agents are blocked on right now) from being held up by an open-ended hardening pass on a different feature.

## User impact
- (1)/(3): a malicious or buggy caller could write outside the intended jobs/log directories.
- (2): backend subprocesses can still leak/orphan in a narrow race window despite the #160 fix.
- (4): `review status`/`review wait` become unusable for a job whose bookkeeping landed in the temp-dir fallback, once the original process has exited.

## Cost of inaction
Sandboxed/shared-machine callers of `--detach` keep hitting confusing "no such job" errors or (rarer) a subtle security gap, without a clear diagnosis path.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `write_job`/`_job_lock_path` validate the job-id BEFORE any filesystem call.
- [ ] A regression test signals a real in-flight `_run_streamed` between spawn and registration and asserts no orphan survives.
- [ ] `_fallback_log_dir()`/`jobs_dir()`'s temp-dir tier verifies ownership (and rejects a symlink) before trusting a pre-existing path at the predictable location.
- [ ] `review status`/`review wait` can find a job whose bookkeeping fell back to the temp-dir tier, from a FRESH process that didn't inherit the spawning process's environment.

## Screenshots
(none — CLI/security hardening, not a UI change)

comments.body:
Additional findings from a 3rd review pass (still dogfooding #162, these are all #160/detach-scope, not #162):

5. `kill_live_children()` only reaps `_run_streamed`'s registered children — the QA web/bot/ext harnesses (`reviewlib/qa/web_harness.py`, `bot_harness.py`, `ext_harness.py`) also spawn `start_new_session=True` subprocesses but never register them, so SIGTERM/the backstop can still orphan those.
6. `--detach` is accepted for every management command (`jobs`, `wait`, `install-skill`, `install-commit-hook`), not just review modes — `_spawn_detached_job` only special-cases dashboard/spec-web.
7. A freshly-created job record is written as `status="running"` with no `pid` yet — a concurrent `review status`/reconciliation pass in that narrow window can misreport it as `unknown-terminated`.
8. `backstop._fire()` runs QA teardown synchronously before writing the detached job's terminal status — a slow teardown can lose to the 3s deadman timer, so the job never gets its accurate exit code (e.g. 124) recorded.
9. `tests/test_detach_jobs.py::test_detach_returns_immediately_with_job_id` doesn't wait for or kill its spawned child before the tmp dir context exits — can leak a process that races later tests.

Not blocking #162 (the log/jobs-dir sandboxed-write fallback, already fixed and shipped) — tracked here since they're the same `--detach`/job-tracking feature area (#160).

Update after actually fixing the 4 original P2s in PR #164 (per explicit instruction to close them out rather than defer): 3 of the 4 are now genuinely fixed (job-id validation ordering, detached log-path recording, QA-harness reaper coverage across all 4 SUT-spawning sites). The 4th (cross-process job-directory discovery) turned out to be a genuine rabbit hole — 4 rounds of review surfaced progressively deeper issues in the "pointer file" mitigation:

1. Basic cross-process discovery via a pointer file + lock (fixed).
2. Symlink/foreign-ownership attacks on the pointer file and its lock (fixed — O_NOFOLLOW + uid checks both ways).
3. Asymmetric-sandbox scenario (a `--detach` spawn hits the fallback tier, but a LATER `review status` call's sandbox has widened so it never even looks at the pointer) — partially fixed: `read_job`/`list_jobs` now check a secondary pointer-recorded directory, but ONLY when `$REVIEW_JOBS_DIR` is not explicitly set (an override must stay isolated, never silently widened — this was itself a real bug in my first attempt at #3, which ignored the override and could leak unrelated job records/argv across an intentional isolation boundary).
4. Still open, explicitly NOT fixed in #164 (this is where I stopped per the "don't force a bad partial fix" instruction): the pointer only ever tracks the SINGLE most-recent fallback directory. If a process's fallback directory rotates (pointer overwritten by a new mkdtemp), any job still running in the PREVIOUS fallback directory becomes permanently undiscoverable to `review status`/`review jobs` — they only ever look at the pointer's current value. A real fix needs either a small append-only index of every fallback directory ever used, or a different design entirely (e.g. a stable non-random last-resort location instead of `mkdtemp()`). Also open: `_secondary_jobs_dir()`'s validation of a candidate directory requires it be WRITABLE (`probe_writable_dir`), which is stricter than necessary for a READ — a directory that's readable but no longer writable (permissions narrowed, not widened) is incorrectly rejected even though the records in it could still be read.

Both of these need an actual design decision, not a patch — that's why they're staying here rather than becoming round 5 of the same PR.

Round 4/5 update on the cross-process job-directory discovery item (the one I flagged as needing a real design, not a patch):

Codex found yet another gap in the SAME area: \`_secondary_jobs_dir()\` only ever consults the pointer file, which is written ONLY by the rarer \`mkdtemp()\` last-resort tier. The FAR more common fallback tier — the FIXED per-uid temp directory (\`/tmp/review-cli-jobs-<uid>\`, tried before ever reaching \`mkdtemp()\`) — writes no pointer at all, so if a \`--detach\` job's bookkeeping lands there while the standard cache dir is unwritable, and the standard dir becomes writable again before a later \`review status\`/\`review jobs\` call, that later call switches to the standard dir and STILL can't find the job (the exact same class of bug the pointer was built to fix, just for a different fallback tier the pointer mechanism doesn't cover).

This is the 5th round of finding a new gap in the same "one pointer file records one fallback location" design. I'm treating this as confirmation, not a new item: the real fix here is NOT another patch on top of the pointer mechanism (extending it to cover more tiers just adds another layer with its own edge cases) — it needs an actual index of every directory `jobs_dir()` has EVER resolved to in this fallback family (fixed-uid dir, AND any mkdtemp dirs), checked on every read, OR a fundamentally different mechanism (e.g. a single well-known non-random path used for ALL tiers, so there's only ever one place to look, never a "which of N directories is it in this time" question).

Stopping here per the "don't force a bad partial fix" instruction — this needs a deliberate design pass, which I'd rather scope as dedicated follow-up work on this ticket than keep re-patching one-tier-at-a-time. The core log/jobs-dir sandboxed-write fix (#162) itself does not depend on this — a `--detach` job whose bookkeeping fell back to ANY of these tiers still runs and completes correctly; the only user-visible effect of this remaining gap is that `review status`/`review jobs` can occasionally report "no such job" for one that's actually fine, in the specific case where the sandbox's writable-directory situation changed BETWEEN the spawn and the status check.

Follow-up from PR #164's third review round (Codex), same "hand-edited / stale job record" class as the items already tracked here. #164 now skips non-object JSON and records without a well-formed `job_id` (`read_job` / `list_jobs`), and made `main`'s finalizer write best-effort. Still open, deliberately left out of #164 (the only writer of these files is review-cli itself, so none of this is reachable without editing a record by hand):

- `review jobs`: a dict record whose `status` is not a string (`{"job_id": "<valid>", "status": []}`) raises `TypeError` in the `:<18` table formatting (`reviewlib/cli.py`, `_jobs_subcommand`); a string `started_at` makes the mixed-type sort fail.
- `review status <id>`: a record file holding `{}` passes `read_job` (it is a dict), `job_status` returns it unchanged, and `_status_subcommand` indexes `rec["job_id"]` -> `KeyError`.

Fix shape: validate the fields the CLI consumes (`job_id`, `status` string, numeric `started_at`/`finished_at`) once in `read_job`/`_is_well_formed_record`, and add malformed-object cases next to `test_jobs_listing_skips_schema_malformed_records`.

One more from the same PR's acceptance proof: a single `review diff --detach` run whose jobs dir is unwritable prints the `[review-cli] cannot create/write jobs dir … falling back to a temp dir` warning 7 times (the fallback PATH is memoized in `jobs.jobs_dir()`, the stderr warning is not). Print it once per process.

title: Test-ordering flakes: 4 tests fail under full pytest suite but pass in isolation (pre-existing on main)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
While validating [PR #167](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/167) (opencode/grok panel seat) we found 4 tests fail when the full pytest suite runs in default order but pass individually: 3 in [tests/test_review_commit_checkpoint.py](tests/test_review_commit_checkpoint.py) and 1 in [tests/test_reviewer_board.py](tests/test_reviewer_board.py). Reproduced identically on unmodified main (checked out clean, no changes from that PR applied) -- so this is pre-existing test pollution, not something introduced by that PR. [tests/smoke.py](tests/smoke.py)'s test_dashboard_managed_surface_and_lib_absent_fallback also fails under the full suite and also reproduces on main; it may share the same root cause or may be a separate environment-dependent dashboard-service flake -- needs its own investigation to confirm which.

## User impact
Anyone running the full test suite on this project -- a contributor before opening a PR, or a reviewer checking someone else's pull request such as [PR #167](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/167) -- sees 4 tests fail even though nothing is actually broken. They then have to stop and manually re-run each failing test by itself to figure out it was a false alarm, which wastes their time on every single PR, not just this one. If this keeps happening, people will eventually stop trusting a red test run at all and might miss a PR that has a genuine bug.

## Cost of inaction
Every future PR's full-suite test run keeps showing these same 4 false failures, and each contributor or reviewer re-diagnoses them from scratch or starts ignoring red runs altogether, which risks a real bug slipping through unnoticed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Full pytest suite (pytest with default/full ordering) passes 100% on main with zero failures, run twice in a row with different random seeds if pytest-randomly is used; test_review_commit_checkpoint.py's 3 failing tests and the failing test_reviewer_board.py test each pass both in isolation (pytest path::test) and inside the full suite
- [ ] Root cause documented: identify the specific shared or global state (module-level singleton, unreset fixture, leaked file-system or environment state, or class-level cache) that differs between isolated and full-suite runs for [tests/test_review_commit_checkpoint.py](tests/test_review_commit_checkpoint.py) and [tests/test_reviewer_board.py](tests/test_reviewer_board.py), and fix it (reset in a fixture/teardown) or isolate the test (tmp_path, dependency injection) rather than reordering tests to hide it; [tests/smoke.py](tests/smoke.py)'s test_dashboard_managed_surface_and_lib_absent_fallback investigated and either confirmed as the same root cause or filed/fixed separately with its own explanation

title: test: leaked backend_available monkeypatch in test_run_stats.py corrupts later tests under non-default ordering
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The board-resolver test helper in [test_run_stats.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/tests/test_run_stats.py) saves the backend-availability stub AFTER it was already patched to always-true by a shared helper, then restores that already-patched value in its own finally block AFTER the shared helper's own restore ran — permanently leaving the availability check patched to always-true for the rest of the pytest process.

title: review-cli: flat review path can pass and checkpoint on rc=0-but-unusable output (pre-existing)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Codex flagged this (P1) while reviewing the provider-failover fix on PR 157/161: [mode_review](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/modes/review.py) returns the final unusable result unchanged after exhausting providers, but the caller's ok check only looks at returncode being zero, not whether the result is actually usable. Confirmed via git blame this exact ok-check line predates the whole provider-failover feature (present unchanged since before PR 157/161 started), so it is a real but PRE-EXISTING bug, not something the failover work introduced -- out of scope for that PR's narrow fix.

## User impact
A flat review whose every seat responds with an empty body or an explicit unavailable marker but a zero exit code is silently treated as a passing review: with --staged it writes the review-passed stamp, and with --staged --commit it can create a real checkpoint commit, even though no reviewer actually produced a usable verdict.

## Cost of inaction
The pre-commit review gate and the --commit checkpoint feature can both be satisfied by a review that never actually reviewed anything, defeating the point of the gate without any visible error.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The flat -m review path's success/tally check in [mode_review](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/modes/review.py) uses result_is_usable instead of a bare returncode==0 check, so a seat that exits 0 with no real verdict can no longer satisfy --staged stamping or --commit checkpointing.
- [ ] A regression test drives the flat path with a fake backend that returns returncode 0 and an empty or sentinel body for every provider, and asserts the overall run is NOT treated as ok (no stamp, no checkpoint, nonzero exit).

title: review-cli: board failover reuses the original route's per-provider effort after a mid-review provider switch
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Codex flagged this (P2) while reviewing the provider-failover fix on PR 157/161: the flat path (fixed in that PR) now resolves effort from whichever concrete provider actually runs, but the board path's mid-review failover only replaces the seat's model on switch and keeps carrying the ORIGINAL route's effort value, so a per-route --effort override can apply to the wrong (pre-switch) route after a failover.

## User impact
A per-provider --effort override intended to size whichever backend actually executes (e.g. giving opencode seats a bigger reasoning budget) can silently apply the WRONG route's effort level once a board seat fails over mid-review, producing an inconsistent reasoning budget between the flat and board paths for the same failover scenario.

## Cost of inaction
The two review paths (flat -m and the reviewer board) disagree on how effort is resolved after failover, which is confusing and could under- or over-provision reasoning effort for a switched-over seat without any visible signal.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The board path's mid-review failover in [panel.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/panel.py) re-resolves the run-scoped per-provider effort override for the NEW provider after a failover switch, instead of keeping the original seat's effort value from before the switch.
- [ ] A regression test drives a board seat that fails over from one route to another (e.g. z.ai direct to its opencode alternate) under a per-provider --effort override for both routes, and asserts the dispatched effort matches the ACTUALLY-running route, mirroring the flat-path parity test already added for this in PR 157/161.

title: review-cli: last-working-provider cache eligibility should use the unfiltered chain, not the availability-filtered one
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Codex flagged this (P2) while reviewing the provider-failover fix on PR 157/161: cache_eligible is computed from len(chain) > 1 where chain is the AVAILABILITY-FILTERED list passed into provider_chain, so if the cached provider happens to be the sole route that currently passes preflight, the filtered chain collapses to length 1 and forget_working_provider is skipped on failure -- the stale failed provider then gets re-promoted to the front the next time another provider recovers.

## User impact
When someone is running reviews at a moment when only one of a model's backends is reachable, and that one backend then fails, review-cli forgets to clear its memory of it -- so the next time a second backend comes back online, review-cli still tries the one that JUST failed first, wasting one extra retry before it self-corrects.

## Cost of inaction
The last-working-provider cache can get stuck recommending a recently-failed provider in this specific narrow-availability window, undermining the cache's whole purpose (avoiding a repeat failover) exactly when it would matter most.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] cache_eligible in both [panel.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/panel.py) and [review.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/modes/review.py) is derived from the length of the model's FULL configured provider chain (before availability filtering), not the length of the chain after dropping currently-unreachable providers.
- [ ] A regression test seeds the cache with a provider that is the ONLY one passing preflight availability at the time, makes that provider then fail at runtime, and asserts forget_working_provider still runs so the stale entry is cleared once another provider recovers.

(none)

title: review-cli: consolidate the duplicated provider-failover liveness predicate and state machine
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Fable flagged this (P1, design) while reviewing PR 157/161's provider-failover fixes: the invariant that the guard, the ETA plan, and the real dispatch split must agree on liveness is currently enforced by copy-paste plus comments across two files and two different name-resolution styles, which is the exact class of drift the original bug was. The flat path's failover loop is also a full second copy of the board path's loop, and the two copies have already diverged in three observable ways (result identity, switch-over observability, exception normalization).

## User impact
Right now two people fixing a provider-failover bug in one of these two copies (the board path or the flat -m path) can each believe they fixed it everywhere, while the other copy quietly keeps the old, wrong behavior -- exactly what happened with the P1s just fixed in PR 157/161.

## Cost of inaction

title: P0: codex backend recursively re-invokes 'review diff' via unrestricted shell — unbounded process-spawn loop, machine-hanging (live-reproduced)
body:
## What
reviewlib/backends.py review_codex() invokes the codex CLI with only '-s read-only -C <cwd> --ephemeral' (backends.py:194). That flag is an OS-level filesystem/network sandbox — it restricts writes and default network egress, but does NOT restrict codex's shell/exec tool, which is codex's only interaction mode. It has no equivalent of the Claude backend's '--tools ""' (empty tool allowlist, backends.py:1801 — physically disables all built-in tools including Bash) or the opencode agentic backend's explicit permission block (_READONLY_AGENT_DENIED_PERMISSIONS, backends.py:~228, denies bash/edit/write/webfetch/task/etc). Nothing stops the codex agent from shelling out to an arbitrary read-permitted command — including re-invoking 'review diff' on the same worktree, which itself spawns another codex backend call, forming an unbounded self-reinvocation loop. No recursion guard exists anywhere in the codebase (grepped reviewlib for a reentrancy/active-run env marker — none found).

## Why (motivation)
The codex backend's ONLY safety mechanism is the '-s read-only' sandbox flag, which is a filesystem/network restriction, not a tool restriction. Every other backend in this file pairs its sandbox with an explicit tool-deny: Claude gets '--tools ""' (all built-in tools off) plus a system-prompt instruction as defense-in-depth (_CLAUDE_REVIEW_SYSTEM: 'Do not use tools, inspect files, ask for permissions, or plan tool work' — backends.py:1354-1355); opencode's read-only agent gets an explicit permission block denying bash, edit, write, webfetch, task, todowrite, websearch, lsp, skill. Codex has neither. Its core capability IS running shell commands (that is what 'codex exec' means), so a filesystem-write sandbox alone does not stop it from executing 'review diff' as a plain read-permitted subprocess — no disk write is needed to launch a process.

## User impact
CONFIRMED LIVE while filing this ticket via direct ps ancestry trace on a shared 14-core/24GB dev Mac (2026-08-11 approx 16:44-17:03 local), independently of and in addition to an earlier same-session report of the identical failure. A single review-cli invocation rooted in one worktree of the hyperide repo had been recursing for 8+ hours at snapshot time. Traced pid-to-ppid chain shows an unbroken cycle: codex exec (node wrapper) then codex exec (vendor binary) then review diff (python) then codex exec then codex exec then review diff, repeating, WITH BRANCHING (one codex-exec process observed parenting two separate review-diff children at once) — growth is worse than linear. Machine-wide snapshot at that moment: 40 live 'codex exec -s read-only' processes and 11 live 'review diff' processes spread across four unrelated worktrees and projects, swap at 7245.81MB of 8192MB (88.5 percent used), only about 75MB RAM free, load average 14.24 / 31.29 / 60.36. This corroborates an earlier report in the same session window: a similar pid chain of roughly 5+ hops repeating, with 38 review-diff plus 98 codex-exec processes total, several already orphaned to launchd after 20-28+ minutes unsupervised, machine reported fully hanging/unresponsive by the user, plus an independent report of Codex hanging unresponsive at 0 percent CPU for 17+ minutes during an unrelated review diff attempt in the same window. Any engineer or agent on a shared machine running review diff with the codex backend can silently degrade the machine to near-unresponsive for every other concurrent user, with no indication to the invoking process that anything is wrong (it just looks like a slow review) until swap exhaustion causes unrelated failures.

## Cost of inaction
This is not a rare edge case: 40+ concurrent codex and review processes were observed spontaneously arising across four unrelated projects during ordinary day-to-day agent usage, not a stress test, and at least two independent instances of this exact failure mode occurred in the same session window. Every future review diff or panel run using the codex backend on any repo remains a live fork-bomb risk that can take down a shared dev machine for every concurrent user or session on it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] The codex backend runs with a hard tool/capability restriction equivalent to '--tools ""' or opencode's 'bash: deny' — NOT solely '-s read-only' sandboxing. Verify: launch 'review diff -m codex' against a throwaway repo under a process-count watchdog and confirm zero child processes are ever spawned by the codex process over a multi-minute run. — forced: Verified live 2026-09-09 on main@e765dce: codex backend gets an execpolicy .rules command-level deny, the closest available equivalent to --tools ""/bash:deny (codex has no empty-tool-allowlist flag, confirmed in install.py:416-424 comment). reviewlib/install.py:457-522 install_codex_recursion_guard() writes a Starlark execpolicy .rules file to $CODEX_HOME/rules/ with prefix_rule(...,decision="forbidden") for review/codex/claude/opencode/omp as shell commands (verified via `codex execpolicy check` per install.py:421 comment: decision=forbidden). reviewlib/backends.py:321-343 _ensure_codex_recursion_guard() calls this on every review_codex() invocation. Live-tested: tests/test_codex_recursion_guard_rules.py (12 tests) + tests/test_reentrancy_guard.py::test_review_codex_calls_ensure_codex_recursion_guard (line 273) pass 28/28 today (venv pytest run, 1.47s). NOT a process-count-watchdog live run against a real codex binary (no codex CLI on this box) - this is the documented residual gap: install.py:432-444 explicitly notes execpolicy catches only the literal first-token invocation, not every indirection (bash -c wrapper, absolute path, python3) - which is exactly why criterion 2's REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE guard exists as the layer that DOES catch those (it checks inside review's own process at startup, regardless of how it was invoked).
- [x] A recursion guard is added as defense-in-depth: an env var (e.g. REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE=1) is set before invoking ANY backend (claude, codex, opencode, gemini), and review-cli's own entrypoint (reviewlib/cli.py) checks it on startup and refuses to run (clear error, non-zero exit) if already set — so a regression in the sandboxing fix above still fails closed. — forced: Verified live 2026-09-09 on main@e765dce: REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE reentrancy guard is real and active. reviewlib/cli.py:3167 defines REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE_ENV="REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE". _reject_if_reentrant() (cli.py:3170-3236) checks os.environ.get(...) is not None (line 3224) and refuses with non-zero exit + review-cli#180-referencing message (cli.py:3225-3229) when set, running FIRST in the dispatch chain (cli.py:3683-3691). main()'s guarded dispatch sets os.environ[REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE_ENV]="1" (cli.py:3697) wrapping the ENTIRE dispatch in try/finally (cli.py:3698-3701) before any backend runs, so the marker reaches every backend child. Verified by tests/test_reentrancy_guard.py::test_codex_backend_self_reinvocation_is_blocked_when_guard_is_active (line 348-365): asserts own_env=="1" propagated into a spawned codex-equivalent process, and a nested review invocation from inside it is rejected (rc!=0, stderr contains "review-cli#180"). Live pytest run today: 28/28 pass (venv, 1.47s). Re-checked sequentially after an earlier concurrent write on this same ticket clobbered this criterion's checkbox.
- [x] review-cli enforces a hard ceiling on the process tree it spawns per backend call — either a max-descendant-count check or a real process-group-based timeout kill on the codex/claude/opencode subprocess (reviewlib/backends.py _run_streamed already takes a 'timeout' arg; verify it kills the whole process group, not just the direct child — the observed incident processes include grandchildren that outlived their immediate parent) — so a runaway backend is killed automatically, well under 20 minutes, instead of running unsupervised for hours. — forced: Verified live 2026-09-09 on main@e765dce by reading process.py directly: reviewlib/process.py:1465 spawns every backend child with start_new_session=True (own process group). reviewlib/process.py:_kill_tree(proc, pgid) (lines 1250-1280) does a real process-GROUP kill, not direct-child-only: os.killpg(pgid, SIGTERM) (line 1265 via _signal_group), waits up to 3s (line 1275), then unconditionally os.killpg(pgid, SIGKILL) (line 1280) specifically because "a grandchild in the same group can still be alive and holding the pipe" (docstring lines 1253-1259). _run_streamed (process.py:1283) calls this in its finally block on timeout (idle or wall mode per timeout_mode param, cli.py:1306-1312 docstring) - this bounds any single backend call automatically, no external watchdog needed, and well under the 20-minute bar (default caller timeouts are far below that; idle-timeout default is even tighter). Additionally reviewlib/process.py:290-297 maintains a _LIVE_CHILDREN registry of (proc,pgid) so an external SIGTERM/backstop can also drain and _kill_tree every live child even if the parent process itself dies via os._exit (comment lines 428-435 explains why this registry exists: os._exit skips the normal finally path). No process-count/max-descendant cap exists (the OTHER half of the criterion's either/or) - only the process-group timeout-kill half is implemented, which the criterion text explicitly accepts as sufficient ("either...or a real process-group-based timeout kill").
- [x] A regression test stubs the codex binary to attempt self-reinvocation (spawn 'review' or 'codex exec' again) and asserts review-cli detects and blocks it via the recursion guard. — forced: Verified live 2026-09-09 on main@e765dce: tests/test_reentrancy_guard.py has the regression test pair the criterion asks for. test_codex_backend_self_reinvocation_is_blocked_when_guard_is_active (lines 348-365) stubs a fake codex-equivalent binary via _run_review_codex_with_fake_binary(tmp, record) that itself attempts a nested `review --help` self-reinvocation, runs it with REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE=1 set (simulating being invoked from inside main()'s guarded dispatch, as it always is in production), and asserts the nested call's returncode != 0 and its stderr contains "review-cli#180" (lines 362-365) - i.e. asserts review-cli detects and blocks the self-reinvocation via the recursion guard, exactly as specified. test_codex_backend_self_reinvocation_control_succeeds_without_the_guard (lines 368-382) is the paired control: same fake binary, same nested call, but with REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE unset - asserts rc==0, proving the block above is attributable to the guard and not to the fake binary/tempdir/some unrelated failure. Live pytest run today confirms both pass: 28/28 total in tests/test_reentrancy_guard.py + tests/test_codex_recursion_guard_rules.py (venv, 1.47s, exit 0).

title: Surface rate-limit reset time and suggest retry timer on backend usage-limit errors
body:
## What
When a backend call fails with a rate-limit or usage-limit error, review-cli should parse any reset timestamp, retry-after header, or equivalent quota-refresh field present in that backend's API error response and print it clearly in the error output, instead of a generic failure message. The output should also explicitly recommend that the user/agent set a timer or reminder to retry after the reset time, framing the failure as a transient, self-resolving condition rather than a hard block that requires a different resolution path (e.g. escalating to a human or switching backends).

## Why (motivation)
Incident: the Codex GitHub bot integration hit a usage limit while reviewing a PR. The error message did not make clear WHEN the limit would reset, which led to unnecessary escalation and confusion about whether a human decision was needed — when in fact the quota refreshed naturally within a few hours and a simple wait-and-retry would have resolved it with zero human involvement.

## User impact
Agents and humans currently cannot tell, from review-cli's own output, whether a rate-limit failure is a permanent stop-the-world problem or a transient one that self-resolves shortly. This wastes human attention on escalations that a timer could have handled, and risks agents giving up on a backend (or switching backends) when simply waiting would have worked.

## Cost of inaction
Every future rate-limit hit repeats the same ambiguity: agents either escalate to a human unnecessarily (wasting the human's time, as happened in the referenced incident) or treat the backend as dead and route around it, when the correct action was to wait a bounded, known amount of time and retry automatically.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given a backend error response that includes a machine-readable reset time (timestamp, retry-after header, or similar field), review-cli's error output displays the parsed reset time in human-readable form (e.g. absolute time and/or a relative countdown).
- [ ] Given a backend error response with NO reset-time information available, review-cli falls back to today's existing generic rate-limit message unchanged (no regression for backends that don't expose this data).
- [ ] The error output text explicitly suggests retrying after the reset time (e.g. 'this backend will likely recover on its own — consider retrying after <time>') instead of implying the run is permanently blocked.

title: review-cli: wire real token/cost capture for the 4 agentic CLI backends (codex/opencode/omp/claude) via their --json modes
body:
## What
Each of the 4 CLI-subprocess-backed harnesses (codex, opencode, omp, claude in CLI mode) exposes exact token usage AND cost in its own structured-output mode, verified live on 2026-08-14: codex exec --json emits a turn.completed event with usage:{input_tokens,cached_input_tokens,output_tokens,reasoning_output_tokens}; opencode run --format json emits step_finish.tokens:{total,input,output,reasoning,cache:{read,write}} plus a cost field; omp --mode json emits a usage object with a nested cost; claude -p --output-format json emits top-level usage, total_cost_usd, and a per-model modelUsage[model].costUSD breakdown. review-cli's review stat command (this same investigation's deliverable) currently reports tokens: not captured for all 4 because review-cli invokes each CLI in its plain human-readable-stdout mode, not the JSON mode. Switching to the JSON mode is NOT a small additive change: it replaces the CLI's readable stdout wholesale, and review-cli's live tail -f logging plus its existing paywall/auth/context-pollution detection all scan that readable stdout as prose today. Also note codex is invoked with --ephemeral (no on-disk session persistence), so there is no post-hoc session-transcript file to read as an alternative for that backend. This needs a real design: either run the JSON mode and reconstruct a human-readable transcript plus re-anchor every body-substring signal on the JSON structure instead, or capture usage via a second lightweight mechanism without disturbing today's live-streamed dispatch.

## Why (motivation)
The 2026-08 token-burn investigation that built review stat found real per-call cost signals exist in all 4 agentic CLIs' own output but are silently thrown away today because review-cli parses only their plain-text stdout; review stat currently has to report tokens as not captured for the 4 backends that are the large majority of real call volume

## User impact

title: seat_cooldown: cooldown store keyed by model only, not (model, transport)
body:
## What

`reviewlib.seat_cooldown`'s cross-invocation cooldown store is keyed by `model` alone, and `active_cooldown()`/`record_cooldown()` are checked BEFORE `REVIEW_CLAUDE_MODE`/CLI-vs-API transport selection in `backends.review_claude`.

## Why (motivation)

A session-limit cooldown recorded from the CLI transport (subscription quota exhausted) also skips that SAME model's separately-billed API transport for the rest of the cooldown window — even though switching transport is a legitimate, immediate fix a human could make (unlike a bare auth failure, which this module already protects against caching). This was flagged as a known limitation in the module's own docstring during the 2026-08 token-burn investigation (review stat / diff-cap / Fable-cooldown feature) but deliberately deferred as out of scope for that change.

## User impact

An operator who notices the CLI-transport Fable seat is cooling down and deliberately sets `REVIEW_CLAUDE_MODE=api` (switching to the key-billed API transport, which has its own separate quota) to keep working still gets skipped for the remainder of the CLI-recorded cooldown window — their explicit transport switch is silently ignored until the window expires or they manually clear it.

## Cost of inaction

An operator's legitimate, immediate workaround (switching transport) keeps silently not working for up to the full cooldown window (default 10 minutes, `$REVIEW_SEAT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS`), with no error message explaining why — they either wait it out unnecessarily or have to know to run `$REVIEW_SEAT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS=0` to un-stick it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cooldown store is keyed by `(model, transport)` instead of `model` alone, where `transport` is resolved the same way `review_claude` itself resolves it (CLI vs API) — a CLI-recorded cooldown no longer blocks that model's API transport, and vice versa.
- [ ] A regression test pins that recording a cooldown under one transport does NOT suppress a dispatch attempt under the other transport for the same model.

## Skipped gates

- links: descriptive text (transport, cooldown keying), not repo/path references

title: seat_cooldown: read-modify-write across record_cooldown/clear_cooldown not locked (lost-update race)
body:
## What
`reviewlib.seat_cooldown.record_cooldown()`/`clear_cooldown()` each do a `_load()` then `_write()` — the individual `_write()` call is atomic (`tempfile.mkstemp` + `os.replace`), but the read-modify-write PAIR across the two calls is not locked as a unit.

## Why (motivation)
A board dispatches its seats in parallel THREADS within one process. Two threads recording a cooldown for TWO DIFFERENT models in the same round can both read the store before either writes — the second thread's write then doesn't include the first thread's new entry, silently dropping it ("last-writer-wins", not corruption). Documented as an accepted, bounded limitation in the module's docstring during the 2026-08 token-burn investigation but deliberately deferred as lower-severity.

## User impact
When two Claude-provider seats in the same board round both hit a chronic session-limit response at the same time, only ONE of their cooldowns reliably persists — the other seat's cooldown record can be silently lost, so the next `review` invocation pays for one more real (and likely still-failing) dispatch for that seat than it should have.

## Cost of inaction
The cooldown feature's core promise (skip a known-dead seat's real dispatch on the next invocation) intermittently fails under the exact concurrent-board condition it's meant to help with most, with no visible error — it just looks like the cooldown "didn't work that time," which is hard to diagnose without knowing this race exists.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The read-modify-write in `record_cooldown`/`clear_cooldown` is protected by a file lock (e.g. `fcntl.flock` on the store file, or an equivalent cross-thread/cross-process lock) so two concurrent recordings for different models never lose either entry.
- [ ] A regression test reproduces the race (multiple threads recording cooldowns for different models concurrently) and asserts every model's cooldown is present afterward, not just the constructed no-corruption guarantee already pinned by `test_concurrent_writes_from_multiple_threads_never_corrupt_the_store`.

## Screenshots

title: review-before-commit gate: exact staged-diff hash has zero tolerance for trivial follow-up edits, forcing a full multi-model re-review on every restage
body:
## What
The pre-commit review-before-commit gate (review-gate script, deployed from agent-tools' git-hooks/global-dispatcher/hooks/review-gate at core.hooksPath, backed by review-cli's _write_review_stamp/_stamp_if_staged_commit_review in reviewlib/install.py and reviewlib/modes/review.py) computes h=$(git diff --no-ext-diff --cached | shasum -a 256) and only allows the commit when that exact hash is found in the single-line .git/review-stamp file. review diff --staged OVERWRITES review-stamp with sha256(current diff text) only on a full, non-degraded, non-truncated review pass. Because SHA-256 has no locality, ANY change to the staged diff -- even a one-line docstring fix, a whitespace change, or re-staging after a trivial follow-up -- produces a completely different hash with zero overlap with the previous one, so the gate has NO notion of 'this is basically the same diff I already reviewed, plus a 3-line tweak'. There is no partial-credit, subset, or delta-based path at all: every restage requires a brand-new full multi-model review round (all configured seats) from scratch.

## Why (motivation)
A background agent implementing [issue #199](https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/199) in sme-archiving-gc got stuck for 3+ hours across 9 full multi-model review rounds. Each round was triggered by a tiny, already-in-scope follow-up fix (the kind of thing normal development produces constantly) that required restaging, which changed the diff's SHA-256 hash and completely invalidated the single stamped hash in .git/review-stamp -- even though the vast majority of the diff was byte-for-byte identical to what had just passed full review minutes earlier. Each fresh round costs roughly 10-20 minutes of wall-clock time across multiple model seats, so the hash-based all-or-nothing check turns cheap, low-risk edits into the single biggest source of wasted time in the review-gated commit workflow.

## User impact
Right now, anyone (human or agent) fixing a typo, a docstring, or a one-line bug after a diff has already passed full review has to sit through another entire multi-model review pass -- often 10 to 20 minutes -- before they are allowed to commit at all, even though almost nothing about the change is actually new. This makes small, safe cleanups expensive to make, which either wastes a lot of time waiting or quietly pushes people toward skipping careful review to avoid the wait.

## Cost of inaction
Every follow-up fix after an initial review continues to cost a full 10-20 minute multi-model review round regardless of how trivial the change is, multiplying total review time by however many small fixes a change needs (observed: 9 rounds for one ticket) and creating real pressure to bypass the gate (git commit --no-verify) just to make progress, which defeats the purpose of mandatory review.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Given a staged diff D that was already fully reviewed and stamped, when the developer/agent makes a small follow-up edit (e.g. under a configurable line-count threshold, such as <=10 changed lines) and restages, then the gate accepts the commit without requiring a brand-new full multi-model review round -- either by computing a hash that tolerates the small delta, or by exposing an explicit opt-in such as review diff --staged --allow-minor-fixup that verifies the new diff is a superset/refinement of the last-reviewed diff plus a small delta and re-stamps without re-dispatching every seat. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/gh208-acceptance-proof.md)
- [x] Given a staged diff D2 that differs from the last-reviewed D1 by MORE than the configured trivial-delta threshold (e.g. a genuinely new code path, not just a fixup), when the developer restages, then the gate still requires a full fresh multi-model review round -- the exception must not become a blanket bypass for substantive changes. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/gh208-acceptance-proof.md)

title: review-cli#208 delta-tolerance: stale baseline survives commits + gate-twin divergence (review follow-ups)
body:
## Summary

`review-cli#208`'s trivial-follow-up delta tolerance (the pre-commit gate's
`_TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK` in `reviewlib/install.py`) shipped with a sound core
counting mechanism, but a Fable review pass on the shipping PR found real gaps
in how the feature behaves *between* commits and across the two deployment
copies of the gate script. None of these block #208 itself — they are
follow-up hardening, filed here instead of expanding that PR's scope.

## Findings (from the #208 PR review, not yet acted on)

1. **High (security/design) — stale baseline survives the commit.** Nothing
   invalidates `review-stamp` / `review-stamp-diff` once the reviewed change is
   actually committed. The commit empties the staged diff, but the companion
   baseline file stays behind, and the gate keeps comparing every *future*
   staged diff against it. If the last reviewed diff was itself small, any
   brand-new unrelated small change can sail through with zero review — and
   keep doing so on every subsequent commit, since the baseline never moves
   forward except via a real `review diff --staged` pass. This contradicts the
   "not a sliding window" invariant `_TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK`'s own comment
   claims. Fix direction: bind the baseline to the commit it was reviewed
   against (record `git rev-parse HEAD` alongside the stamp and require it to
   match current `HEAD`), or clear both stamp files from a post-commit hook.

2. **Medium — hash stamp and companion diff can desynchronize.**
   `_write_review_stamp` writes the hash, then best-effort writes the
   companion diff text in a second step. If the companion write fails (or a
   future writer touches one file and not the other), a fresh hash stamp can
   sit next to a *previous* review's baseline text, and the gate silently
   measures drift against the wrong review. Fix direction: have
   `_TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK` verify `shasum -a 256 "$stamp_diff"` matches the
   hash stamp before trusting it as a baseline (this also subsumes the
   pre-#208-stamp fallback case).

3. **Medium — the "byte-identical twin" gate script has diverged.** The test
   suite's docstring says `_PRECOMMIT` has a byte-identical twin at
   `agent-tools/git-hooks/global-dispatcher/hooks/review-gate`, and
   `install_commit_hook()` delegates to rig (prints "rig owns the global git
   hooks", returns 0) when that twin is active. #208 grows `_PRECOMMIT`
   substantially without touching the twin in the same change, so a
   rig-managed install keeps the old exact-hash-only gate while a direct
   install gets the new tolerance — and `install-commit-hook` reports success
   either way, with no signal that the two diverge. At minimum the twin needs
   the same block added in lockstep; better, factor `_TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK`
   into one generated source both repos consume instead of duplicating the
   shell text.

4. **Low — no audit trail for an accepted trivial follow-up.** The fast path
   is a bare `exit 0`; a one-line stderr notice ("review gate: accepted N-line
   delta over reviewed baseline, threshold M") would make it possible to later
   reconstruct which commits skipped a fresh review — useful context given
   findings 1–2 above.

5. **Low — duplicated plumbing in the stamp writers.**
   `_write_review_stamp_diff` re-runs the same `git rev-parse --git-path`
   subprocess with the same env/exception handling its caller
   (`_write_review_stamp`) just executed. Resolving the git-path once and
   writing both files from one place would also make the write-ordering
   coherence fix from finding 2 easy to enforce in a single spot.

6. **Low — a pre-existing test assertion is weaker than its own premise.**
   `test_length_changing_followup_on_multi_hunk_committed_file_is_still_trivial`
   asserts `baseline_diff.count("\n@@ ") + baseline_diff.startswith("@@ ") >= 1`,
   but the test's premise (metadata delta of 11 under the pre-#208
   implementation) depends on there being exactly 3 shifted hunks. If git ever
   coalesces the hunks, the test would pass vacuously. Should assert the hunk
   count is exactly 3.

7. **Low — large-diff capacity edge in `/bin/sh`.** `_TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK`
   holds the entire diff-of-diffs in a shell variable
   (`diff_out=$(diff -U0 ...)`). For a multi-megabyte staged diff this is
   fragile under a minimal `/bin/sh`. Writing the `diff` output to a second
   temp file and piping through `tail`/`grep` instead would avoid holding it
   all in a variable, while keeping the `diff_rc` exit-code check.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Finding 1 (stale baseline across commits) has a fix or an explicit,
      documented decision not to fix it, with the tradeoff written down.
- [ ] Finding 2 (hash/companion desync) is fixed or explicitly deferred with
      reasoning recorded.
- [ ] Finding 3 (agent-tools twin divergence) is either fixed (twin updated in
      lockstep, or the shell block shared from one source) or filed as its own
      cross-repo ticket if it needs agent-tools-side coordination.
- [ ] Findings 4–7 triaged: fixed, or explicitly deferred with reasoning.

## User impact if not fixed

Findings 1–2 mean the delta-tolerance feature can, in the worst case, let a
sequence of small *unrelated* and never-reviewed changes land on top of one
old genuine review, silently — which is a materially different (weaker)
guarantee than "only a small trailing follow-up on the SAME change is
tolerated," which is what the feature was built and documented to provide.
Finding 3 means an operator who believes `install-commit-hook` gave them the
new tolerance may actually still be on the old exact-hash-only gate with no
error telling them so.

Context: review-cli#208, PR fixing it (delta-tolerance counting fix + 2 new
test cases), review task REVIEW-208.

title: Trivial-delta gate (#208): stale companion desync, SHA-256 gitlink width, mktemp portability
body:
## What
Three follow-up findings from Opus reviewing REVIEW-208 rounds 1-5 together (the pre-commit gate's REVIEW_TRIVIAL_DELTA_LINES tolerance in reviewlib/install.py _TRIVIAL_DELTA_BLOCK), deliberately deferred rather than fixed in the same PR to avoid an unbounded review-fix loop: (1) _write_review_stamp writes the hash stamp before the review-stamp-diff companion and swallows all exceptions on the companion write, so a partial-write failure (e.g. ENOSPC) after the hash succeeds leaves a STALE companion from a prior baseline; the gate never checks the companion's hash matches the current stamp before trusting it as the diff baseline, so drift could be measured against the wrong (older) baseline. (2) the k3 binary/gitlink fail-closed pre-check anchors Subproject commit lines to a 40-hex-char sha, which only matches SHA-1 repos; a SHA-256 git repository's 64-hex-char gitlink pointers would not match, so a submodule bump in such a repo would NOT fail closed and could read as a trivial 2-line change. (3) the fast-path's mktemp call uses no template, whose portability across sh implementations is not guaranteed; a mktemp failure silently disables the whole tolerance feature (safe direction, just loses the feature, not a security issue).

## Why (motivation)
Found during this feature's own review pass (Opus, correctness/security lens) while dogfooding the pre-commit gate on its own pull request; each finding is the same undercount/bypass class as three earlier fixes already shipped in that same pull request, just lower severity or likelihood (a partial-write race, SHA-256 repositories being rare, mktemp portability being platform-specific), so they were deferred rather than chase an unbounded review-fix loop on one pull request.

## User impact
Without the first fix: in the rare case a machine runs low on disk right when a review writes its stamp, a later restage could be compared against the wrong previously-reviewed diff and a real change could slip through as trivial, unreviewed. Without the second fix: a repository using git's newer SHA-256 object format would not get the fail-closed protection on submodule bumps that SHA-1 repositories already have. Without the third fix: on a stricter or non-GNU shell, the trivial-delta convenience feature could silently stop working (falls back to the safe, pre-existing exact-hash-only behavior, not a security regression, just lost convenience).

## Cost of inaction
The three edge cases stay open; none are reachable in this project's own actual development environment today (normal disk space, SHA-1 repositories, macOS), but they are documented gaps that could surface if the tool is used in other environments (CI runners, SHA-256 repositories) or under disk pressure.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The gate verifies the review-stamp-diff companion's sha256 matches the hash recorded in the review-stamp file before trusting it as the diff baseline; a stale or mismatched companion falls through to the full-review block instead of being silently trusted, with a regression test simulating a stale companion (older baseline) alongside a newer stamp hash.
- [ ] The Subproject-commit fail-closed anchor matches both SHA-1 (40 hex characters) and SHA-256 (64 hex characters) gitlink pointers, with a regression test for a SHA-256-width gitlink bump still failing closed.
- [ ] mktemp has a documented fallback so a bare template-less mktemp failure on a stricter sh implementation does not silently disable the trivial-delta feature.

title: review-gate pre-commit hook mismatches _write_review_stamp's hash when diff.noprefix=true
body:
## What's broken

`~/.config/git/hooks/review-gate` (the pre-commit gate installed by `review install-commit-hook`) permanently fails to recognize a genuinely-reviewed staged diff as reviewed, on any machine with `git config diff.noprefix true` set (globally or per-repo).

## Root cause

Two different code paths compute the "same" diff differently:

- `reviewlib/cli.py:_git_diff` (used both to feed the review prompt AND, via `_write_review_stamp`, to compute the stamp hash) explicitly pins `--src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/` on the `git diff` invocation. This is a deliberate fix, per the function's own docstring, for machines with `diff.noprefix=true` set.
- `~/.config/git/hooks/review-gate` (a shell script, separate from the Python codebase) computes its comparison hash with a plain `command git diff --no-ext-diff --cached | shasum -a 256`, no `--src-prefix`/`--dst-prefix` override, so it inherits the ambient `diff.noprefix` config.

When `diff.noprefix=true`:
- `_git_diff`'s diff has `a/`/`b/` prefixed paths in the `diff --git` header, producing one SHA256.
- The hook's diff has bare (unprefixed) paths in that same header, producing a different SHA256.

The two hashes can never match, so `git commit` always reports "staged changes have not been reviewed", even immediately after a genuinely successful `review diff --staged` run that wrote a stamp.

## Reproduction

1. `git config --global diff.noprefix true` (reproduces the live setting).
2. In any repo with the review-gate hook installed, make a trivial staged change.
3. `review diff --staged --pool 1` succeeds with an "ok" verdict and writes review-stamp.
4. `git commit -m "test"` is blocked: "staged changes have not been reviewed".

Confirmed by hand: `git diff --no-ext-diff --cached --src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/ | shasum -a 256` matches the `review-stamp` file's contents exactly. `git diff --no-ext-diff --cached | shasum -a 256` (no explicit prefix, what the hook actually runs) does not.

## Fix

Pin the same `--src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/` flags in the hash computation inside `~/.config/git/hooks/review-gate`, matching `_git_diff`'s existing fix for this exact `diff.noprefix` footgun. The install/template source for this hook needs the same fix so freshly-installed hooks don't regress.

## Impact

Any developer or machine with `diff.noprefix=true` set (confirmed live on this machine) cannot satisfy the pre-commit review gate normally. Every commit either needs a `--no-verify` bypass (discouraged/forbidden by policy) or a manual toggle of `diff.noprefix` around each commit. Found while shipping unrelated PRs (rig-cli#210, tg-cli#262) in a cross-repo cleanup session — this is a review-cli bug, not specific to either of those repos.

title: review-quorum gate should tolerate an unavailable/flaky model instead of hard-blocking at exactly N distinct models
body:
## What
The review-quorum gate currently requires exactly N (e.g. 3) genuine review passes across N distinct models before it will let a PR ship. When one panel model is temporarily unavailable or repeatedly times out, the count can never reach N and the gate blocks indefinitely, with no self-service way to proceed - only a live human (Telegram) approval each time. The gate should be able to reach its required quorum by substituting another available model for one that is flaky or unavailable, instead of hard-failing on the exact configured model list.

## Why (motivation)
Alex, on Telegram, describing this exact review-quorum mechanism from a different project context: the gate hard-requires 3 genuine passes across 3 distinct models. One model, the oc zai GLM 5.2 seat, periodically times out - not critical on its own, but the gate refuses to pass until exactly 3 clean passes accumulate. review should be able to work even when there are not enough available models - it should dynamically hand off roles to other available models instead. This is directly corroborated by a live instance the same day in the sme-archiving-gc repo: pull request https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/pull/223 (fixing an issue tracked as SME-ISSUE-132) was blocked by review-quorum with a denial of 2 of 3 iterations, 2 of 3 distinct models, listing the models seen as the claude opus 4.8 seat and the zai-org GLM 5.2 seat - one model short of the hard floor of 3, with no self-service override, only the live-Telegram-approval escape hatch.

## User impact
Right now a single flaky or temporarily unavailable model in the review panel can indefinitely block shipping any PR under the review-quorum gate. The only way around it is a live human approval over Telegram, every single time it happens - that does not scale as a routine occurrence and turns an infrastructure hiccup into a manual escalation for every affected PR.

## Cost of inaction
Developers keep hitting the same wall every time a panel model is temporarily unavailable or slow, and have to manually escalate for a live approval each time instead of the gate self-healing by substituting an available model.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] If a configured/expected model in the quorum panel is unavailable or times out repeatedly, the gate substitutes another available model to reach the required distinct-model count, instead of refusing indefinitely while stuck below the floor.

title: Adversarial review-rigor: neutral prompts, evidence requirement, refutation pass, adversarial role blending
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
An audit of review-cli's own review rigor found the tool's prompts and gates were not adversarial enough to reliably catch subtle bugs, and the repo owner asked for all four findings fixed

## User impact
Reviews run through review-cli become more likely to actually catch bugs instead of rubber-stamping a diff, and a ship-gate-critical quorum call gets an extra safety net before a merge decision

## Cost of inaction
review-cli keeps shipping neutral, easily-rubber-stamped reviews with no adversarial pass, so a subtle regression is more likely to slip through the tool that is supposed to catch it

- [ ] DEFAULT_PROMPT instructs every reviewer to actively try to break the change before concluding it's fine, and requires explicit evidence (checked: ... statements) for a clean verdict, not just for findings
- [ ] review quorum has an opt-in --adversarial-check flag that, after a clean verdict, spawns a refutation pass and surfaces any real finding it turns up instead of discarding it
- [ ] REVIEW_ROLES security and tests carry adversarial framing from the security-paranoid-reviewer and skeptical-SRE personas, and all new behavior is covered by tests plus the existing ruff/smoke suite

title: brainstorm: auto-grounding on cwd git diff has no relevance check or provenance disclosure
body:
## What

`review brainstorm "<topic>"` deliberately auto-grounds the panel on the invoking working
directory's `git diff` when no diff is piped in — this is intentional, documented behavior
(`reviewlib/modes/brainstorm.py:160-164`: "An optional grounding diff... the brainstorm is
ABOUT that specific change"; `cli.py`'s own comment: "`--diff` is the explicit opt-in spelling
of the same probe" that already runs by default). The gap is that this auto-grounding has
**(a) no relevance check** against the topic text being asked about, and **(b) no provenance
disclosure** beyond a bare `grounded=diff` flag with no file list. When the topic names a
specific PR by number, the tool never fetches that PR's actual diff (`gh pr diff <n>`) to
compare or prefer — it silently uses whatever `git diff` happens to be sitting in `cwd`, which
may be a completely unrelated file someone left uncommitted.

Code path (`reviewlib/cli.py`, brainstorm dispatch, ~line 4561):

```python
elif diff is None and is_brainstorm:
    # brainstorm picks up the staged (--staged) or working-tree diff as OPTIONAL
    # grounding context so you can brainstorm ABOUT a specific change. The diff is
    # never required: an absent diff / non-repo / git failure degrades to pure
    # ideation (diff == ""). ...
    try:
        diff = _git_diff(cwd, args.staged)
    except RuntimeError:
        diff = ""
```

This probe runs whenever brainstorm has no piped/staged diff already resolved, regardless of
whether `--diff` was explicitly passed (`--diff` is documented as "the explicit opt-in spelling
of the same probe" the code already runs unconditionally in the `is_brainstorm` branch) — it is
not gated on the topic text referencing "this diff" or "the current change." Any uncommitted
content in `cwd` gets included as grounding, no matter what the question is actually about.
(Note: I could not recover which exact invocation — explicit `--diff` or the implicit probe —
either incident below used; no argv/invocation log survives in review-cli's on-disk state. It
doesn't change the underlying gap: both paths converge on the same unconditional
`_git_diff(cwd, ...)` call with no relevance check and no provenance disclosure.)

`review just-ask`/`review quorum` are **not** affected the same way: their diff attachment is
gated behind `args.diff and panel_mode` (cli.py, the `elif diff is None and panel_mode and
args.diff:` branch) — a genuinely explicit opt-in, only reachable if the user typed `--diff`
themselves. Scoping this report to brainstorm's unconditional probe.

## Impact — two real incidents, same root cause, same day (2026-08-24)

Both ran from the same shared checkout, `/Users/ultra/work/hyperide`, which had a real,
deliberately-tracked build file (`client/__canvas_preview__.tsx`, a generated preview/iframe
entrypoint) sitting uncommitted the whole time — grown from 109 lines at `HEAD` to 2,106 lines
in the working tree.

**Incident 1** — `review brainstorm "What should happen with hyperide PR #677/#678, a
project-scoping fix ...?" --task HYP-1124`
(log: `~/Library/Logs/review-cli/20260824T153327_647593Z-brainstorm.md`)

The topic named PR #677/#678 by number (a `server/routes/*.ts`-only diff — verified via
`gh pr diff --name-only` on both, no preview/iframe files touched). The panel instead
discussed `componentRegistry`, `postMessage`, a "2,100-line generated preview/iframe file"
with `@ts-nocheck` and schema `v15` — all real content, but from the unrelated
`client/__canvas_preview__.tsx` working-tree diff, not from PR #677/#678. Round 1 opens by
quoting `client/__canvas_preview__.tsx` lines 1-2 verbatim. This was reported/acted on as if
it were about the two PRs (an agent auto-filed Linear ticket HYP-1327 recommending they be
closed as superseded), and had to be walked back with an explicit correction comment once
someone ran `gh pr diff --name-only` and found no overlap.

**Incident 2** — `review brainstorm "How do we prevent bugs like this from recurring: a VS
Code extension webview crashes ...?" --task HYP-1328`
(log: `~/Library/Logs/review-cli/20260824T164718_134437Z-brainstorm.md`)

Same mechanism, same file: the panel again grounds heavily on
`client/__canvas_preview__.tsx` ("grew from 109 to 2,106 lines," `componentRegistry`,
`@ts-nocheck`, the forgeable `postMessage` channel) — this time genuinely on-topic for
HYP-1328's webview-crash question, so it wasn't caught as a problem here. But it's the same
silent, unscoped auto-grounding as incident 1 — it worked out this time only because the
unrelated uncommitted diff happened to be topically adjacent.

## Why this matters generally

The failure mode isn't "the model hallucinated." The model accurately described real content
it was handed — the tool handed it the wrong content. Nothing in the transcript, header, or
CLI output flags "the diff fed to this panel came from your cwd's working tree, unrelated to
the PR number you typed in the topic." A reader (or a downstream agent acting on the
synthesis) has no signal to catch the mismatch except independently re-deriving the diff and
diffing it against what the panel discussed — expensive, and only caught this time because a
human happened to sanity-check a surprising recommendation.

This will keep recurring for anyone who:
1. Works in a shared checkout with WIP uncommitted changes (very common in this team's
   worktree-heavy workflow), and
2. Runs `review brainstorm` about a *specific, already-identified* PR/ticket/commit rather
   than "the current change."

## Suggested fix (one or more)

- When the topic text contains a PR reference (`#\d+`, a GitHub PR URL, or an explicit
  `--pr <n>`), fetch and ground on *that PR's* diff (`gh pr diff <n>`) instead of — or in
  addition to, clearly labeled — the cwd working-tree diff.
- Always print (and persist in the discussion log header) an explicit, unmissable line
  identifying the diff source and its file list when auto-grounding kicks in, e.g.
  `grounded=diff (cwd working-tree, 1 file: client/__canvas_preview__.tsx, +1997/-0)` — not
  just the current bare `grounded=diff` flag with no file list. This alone would have let the
  agent in incident 1 catch the mismatch in one line instead of walking the whole
  transcript to notice PR #677/#678 was never mentioned by the panel's actual reasoning.
- Consider warning (not blocking) when the auto-grounded diff's file set shares zero overlap
  with any PR number / file path mentioned in the topic text — a cheap heuristic that would
  have flagged incident 1 immediately.

## Evidence

- `client/__canvas_preview__.tsx` in `/Users/ultra/work/hyperide`: tracked, not gitignored,
  109 lines at `HEAD` (blob `29a4e2fc`), 2,106 lines in the working tree as of 2026-08-24.
- Discussion logs (both on this machine, `~/Library/Logs/review-cli/`):
  `20260824T153327_647593Z-brainstorm.md` (incident 1),
  `20260824T164718_134437Z-brainstorm.md` (incident 2).
- `reviewlib/cli.py`, the `is_brainstorm` unconditional `_git_diff(cwd, args.staged)` branch
  (search `grounding context so you can brainstorm ABOUT a specific change`).

title: true_silence_timeout can silently overshoot the caller's explicit per-call timeout budget
body:
## What

## Why (motivation)
review-cli#235's true-silence slice makes `true_silence_timeout` the SOLE pre-first-byte authority once armed, ignoring the caller's requested `timeout`/idle floor entirely until either output arrives or the true-silence deadline fires (this was the deliberate round-4 fix for the opposite bug — a generous true_silence_timeout being unreachable because the smaller idle check won the race first). But every opencode model defaults to `true_silence_timeout_seconds() == 300` (the registry is empty today), so a dispatch invoked with an explicit short `timeout` (e.g. 60s) on a dead/silent seat now runs up to 300s before reap — 5x the requested budget — holding a concurrency-cap slot the whole time. Flagged independently during review-cli#243's review gate (GLM-cc, performance lens).

## User impact
in a fan-out (quorum/brainstorm), the round is gated by the slowest seat; a caller-tightened timeout on one seat no longer bounds that seat's worst case, silently inflating round latency and occupying a concurrency slot 5x longer than requested.

## Cost of inaction
operators who set a short --timeout to bound worst-case latency get a false sense of an upper bound; the true-silence feature can quietly make things slower for short-timeout callers even though its goal is faster reaping of stuck seats.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] decide whether true_silence_timeout should be clamped to the caller's explicitly-requested timeout (effective_ts = min(ts, timeout)) when timeout is the binding, explicitly-requested value -- while still keeping the round-4 fix intact for the case of a registry-driven true_silence_timeout vs. an ambient/default idle floor
- [ ] add a test pinning the maximum acceptable overshoot once a decision is made
- [ ] document the current behavior in the true_silence_timeout docstring / REVIEW_TRUE_SILENCE_SECONDS help text until fixed

## Screenshots
(none)

- review-cli#235, review-cli#243

## Skipped gates

If a caller ever feeds a deadline-clamped idle timeout into review_opencode's _run_streamed calls, a never-talking seat pre-first-byte still runs up to the full true_silence_timeout (default 300s) regardless of how little wall-clock budget the board deadline actually has left -- overrunning the very deadline #228 exists to enforce. title: Board-deadline-clamped true-silence reap can falsely bench a healthy seat's cooldown
body:
## What

## Why (motivation)
review-cli#243's true-silence slice clamps effective_true_silence_timeout to the active board deadline via _clamp_to_board_deadline (same function idle_timeout already uses, review-cli#221/#228/#254). Verified: the _MIN_DEADLINE_CLAMPED_IDLE_FLOOR (~90s) floor lives INSIDE _clamp_to_board_deadline itself, so the clamp's worst case is bounded to ~90s, never a near-zero instant reap -- this rules out the worst-case scenario a round-9 review raised (a guaranteed false bench of a freshly-spawned seat).

A narrower, still-real case remains open: when a seat spawns late in a deadline-pressured board run, the clamp can shrink true_silence_timeout well below its configured value (e.g. from 300s down to the 90s floor). A seat whose first byte would legitimately have arrived at, say, 120s under normal conditions is then reaped as true-silent purely because THIS RUN was deadline-pressured -- not because the seat itself is unhealthy. _record_true_silence_if_needed only sees the bare true_silenced=True flag; it cannot distinguish 'silent for the full configured budget' from 'silent only because this run ran out of board wall-clock budget.'

## User impact
record_cooldown(model, "true-silence timeout") writes a PERSISTENT, ESCALATING, CROSS-INVOCATION bench for a healthy seat, driven by the previous run's deadline pressure rather than the seat's actual health. Note the asymmetry: the ordinary clamped idle reap (rc 124) is transient with no store side effect -- true-silence is the ONLY reap class that mutates the persistent cooldown store, so this fairness problem is unique to review-cli#235's feature.

## Cost of inaction
A seat that is actually healthy can get progressively longer cooldown windows (10min -> 30min -> 2h -> 8h) purely as a side effect of running under deadline pressure repeatedly, reducing board diversity for reasons unrelated to the seat's real reliability.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] decide whether a board-deadline-CLAMPED true-silence reap should record a cooldown at all (a clamped reap is deadline-driven, not seat-health-driven -- arguably it shouldn't escalate the same way an unclamped reap does)
- [ ] if it should still record something, decide whether it should skip escalation (always fail_count=1 / a short flat TTL) rather than participate in the normal escalating schedule
- [ ] thread the 'was this reap clamped?' signal from _run_streamed's result through to _record_true_silence_if_needed so it can make this distinction
- [ ] add a test pinning the chosen behavior: board deadline armed + tight enough to clamp true_silence_timeout below its configured value + a seat that stays silent for the clamped duration -> assert whether/how record_cooldown fires

title: Poll-loop true-silence check has a narrow lock-acquisition-window race (bytes received but not yet recorded)
body:
## What

## Why (motivation)
review-cli#243's true-silence poll branch (reviewlib/process.py) reads activity["got_output"]/activity["last"] WITHOUT holding log_lock (matching the poll loop's existing, pre-existing, explicitly-documented design: "CPython's GIL makes these single-value reads safe enough; stale reads are harmless because the next 0.5s poll sees any newer state"). That tolerance is correct for the ORDINARY idle-timeout check (a stale read only delays a correct reap by up to one 0.5s poll cycle, never causes a wrong one). It is NOT equally safe for the true-silence check specifically: if the drain thread's os.read() returns real bytes but hasn't yet acquired log_lock to record them into activity, and the poll thread evaluates its reap condition in that exact narrow window (bytes received, not yet recorded, AND the deadline has just been crossed using the stale spawn-time last), the poll thread can reap a process that just produced real output -- and unlike the ordinary idle-timeout case, this is NOT self-correcting on the next poll cycle, because the process is already reaped by then. review-cli#243 round 21 (codex) flagged this; round 15's raw-chunk-vs-decoded-text fix closed a related but different, much more likely race (the same lock-protected write firing on undecoded bytes) -- it did not touch this residual, narrower lock-acquisition-window race.

## User impact
In the (very rare, but not impossible) case where a seat's first byte arrives in the exact microsecond-to-millisecond window between os.read() returning and log_lock being acquired, AND that window happens to straddle the true-silence deadline, a genuinely-alive, just-started-talking seat can be reaped and cooldown-benched (escalating, up to 8h) as if it had produced nothing at all.

## Cost of inaction
An extremely rare, hard-to-reproduce false reap + false cooldown bench of a healthy seat. Low probability given the narrow window (uncontended lock acquisition is typically sub-millisecond), but real.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] decide whether this narrow window is worth closing given how rare it is, or whether it should be explicitly documented as an accepted risk (mirroring how the ordinary idle-timeout's own unsynchronized-read tolerance is already documented as accepted)
- [ ] if closing it: evaluate a dedicated synchronization primitive scoped to just the true-silence check (codex's suggestion), or reordering so the poll thread's reap decision re-checks activity one more time immediately before reaping, inside log_lock, to shrink the window to near-zero
- [ ] this is a poll-loop-wide architectural question (the SAME unsynchronized-read pattern underlies the ordinary idle-timeout check too), not something to patch narrowly for true-silence alone -- scope the fix (or the documented-acceptance) accordingly

## Screenshots
(none)
