title: Cooldown key, actual dispatch, and dashboard identity can disagree for a catch-all colon-form model id
body:
## What

## Why (motivation)
`reviewlib.backends.resolve_backend` has a documented catch-all: an UNRECOGNIZED model id (not matching any named backend prefix, including `oc:`/`opencode:`) still routes to `review_opencode` for back-compat with arbitrary `provider/model` selectors. review-cli#243 round 25 (codex) found that for such a catch-all input (e.g. `"custom:model"`, no `oc:`/`opencode:` prefix), `review_opencode` now computes THREE different identities for the same request:

1. `oc_model = model.split(":", 1)[1] if ":" in model else model` -- the string actually passed to the real `opencode -m <oc_model>` CLI dispatch AND embedded in the sidecar log header. For `"custom:model"` this gives `oc_model = "model"`, silently DROPPING the `"custom"` provider segment entirely. This derivation predates review-cli#243 and is not something that PR introduced -- it is a pre-existing dispatch-correctness question independent of the true-silence feature.
2. `canonical_model = _agentic(model)` (added in review-cli#243 round 22, reviewlib/backends.py) -- used as the cooldown-store and model_behavior-registry KEY. For `"custom:model"` this gives `canonical_model = "oc:custom/model"`, which does NOT match what was actually dispatched.
3. The dashboard PARSER resolves the real dispatch's sidecar log header (`opencode -m model`, i.e. whatever `oc_model` was) back to a board id via `_OPENCODE_MODEL_RE` -- for this case, `oc:model`, which matches NEITHER (1) nor (2) exactly (well, it does match the CLI dispatch by construction, but not the cooldown key).

## User impact
For the (rare) case of a model id reaching `review_opencode` via the catch-all -- not the standard, documented `oc:`/`opencode:` prefix -- the cooldown/model_behavior lookup key, the actual CLI command dispatched, and the dashboard's resolved board-seat id can all disagree. A true-silence cooldown recorded under the `canonical_model` key would never be consulted correctly against what the dashboard/board actually track for that seat.

## Cost of inaction
Cooldown escalation and true-silence protection silently do not work correctly for any model id that reaches review_opencode through the catch-all path rather than an explicit `oc:`/`opencode:` prefix. Given this is an edge/back-compat path, low real-world frequency, but a real correctness gap if it's ever hit.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] decide the correct provider-parsing behavior for a catch-all colon-form model id reaching review_opencode (should `"custom:model"` dispatch as `opencode -m custom/model`, `opencode -m model`, or be rejected as unsupported?) -- this is a product/design question, not purely mechanical
- [ ] once decided, make `oc_model` (the actual CLI dispatch derivation) and `canonical_model` (the cooldown/model_behavior key, via `_agentic`) agree on the SAME provider parsing for this case
- [ ] add a regression test for an unrecognized colon-form model routed through the catch-all, asserting the dispatched CLI command, the cooldown key, and the dashboard-resolved board id all agree

body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A correctness review of PR #249 (adversarial review-rigor) found three LOW-severity, explicitly non-blocking gaps. All three are of the exact 'fixture instead of reality' / 'undocumented residual' class that PR #249 itself closed repeatedly elsewhere, so leaving them unrecorded risks re-discovering them later the hard way.

## User impact
If the real run_moderator signature ever drifts, --adversarial-check would crash with a TypeError on exactly the clean-verdict path the feature exists to double-check, and the whole test suite would still pass. The undocumented marker residual can silently pass a ship gate on a genuine refutation phrased with an em-dash separator.

## Cost of inaction
These stay invisible until someone hits them in production: a shipped change that a real refutation should have blocked, or a crash in the adversarial pass that no test would have caught.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] refutation_verdict's docstring documents the decoration-separated dangerous-direction residual (e.g. 'No — REFUTATION FOUND: ...' resolving to not_found) alongside its two existing documented residuals, with a regression test pinning the behavior so it stays visible
- [ ] A test asserts the REAL panel.run_moderator signature accepts round_no (e.g. via inspect.signature), instead of every test stubbing a fake whose signature could drift from reality

title: review-cli: idle_timeout is computed before the concurrency-slot wait, going stale for a queued seat
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
found by an automated PR review on review-cli#243 while reviewing the true-silence clamp-timing fix: idle_timeout_seconds() is called at function entry, before the concurrency-slot wait, so a seat queued for most of a board deadline keeps an idle budget computed as if it started immediately -- pre-existing since review-cli#228, not introduced by review-cli#243, but now more visible because true-silence's OWN clamp was just fixed to recompute post-queue, creating an asymmetry between the two timeouts for the same call

## User impact
a review that's forced to wait its turn (because too many models are already running) can end up allowed to sit unresponsive for far longer than the overall time budget allows, instead of being cut off and replaced promptly like the rest of the review

## Cost of inaction
a queued-then-silent seat can overrun the board deadline by roughly however long it waited in the queue, defeating review-cli#228's own wall-clock enforcement

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] idle_timeout (like true_silence_timeout, fixed in review-cli#243) is (re)computed after the concurrency semaphore is acquired, immediately before spawning the child, not at _run_streamed entry
- [ ] add a cap=1 regression test: queue a second seat behind a long-running first one, have the queued seat emit one byte then go silent, and assert its post-spawn idle budget reflects the remaining board deadline rather than a stale pre-queue value

## What


## Why (motivation)
Investigating a suspected merge-gate bypass on [HYP-1321](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1321) for [hyperide/hyper-saas PR #747](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/747) on 2026-08-27, running the check from main post-merge reported all 4 recorded review iterations as diff_mismatch, even though the real ship-audit.jsonl entry showed decision:authorized and the recorded diff_files near-totally overlapped the actual merged diff. Every future post-merge audit of a PR's review history via --check will keep producing false bypass alarms, training the human and agents to distrust real alarms too (alarm fatigue) or to waste investigation cycles re-deriving the same false-positive explanation.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] [review task <CODE> --check](https://github.com/hyperide/review-cli) run from a clean main after the PR merged and its branch was deleted no longer falsely reports all recorded iterations as diff_mismatch for iterations that did cover the merged content

title: tests/test_failover_pool.py (and similar) write real retry-logs into the live ~/Library/Logs/review-cli, no $REVIEW_LOG_DIR isolation
body:
## What

`tests/test_failover_pool.py`, `tests/test_provider_failover.py`, and `tests/test_board_deadline_wiring.py` exercise `write_retry_log`/`run_seat_with_retry`/`run_board_with_failover` (confirmed via `grep`) but — unlike `tests/test_seat_cooldown.py`'s `_with_store` helper and `tests/test_inseat_retry.py`'s own per-test fixture — never set `$REVIEW_LOG_DIR`. Every such test run writes real `*-retry-NNNN.log` sidecars into the developer's actual `log_dir()` (`~/Library/Logs/review-cli` on macOS), not an isolated temp dir.

Confirmed live on this machine: `~/Library/Logs/review-cli` contains real files like `20260828T180538_267082Z-Fable__architect_-retry-0007.log` with synthetic test-fixture bodies ("boom0", "x", "authentication failed") — these can only have come from a test run, not a real dispatch, since `DEFAULT_BOARD`'s Fable entry ("Fable [architect]") is imported directly by `tests/test_failover_pool.py`.

## Why (motivation)

`tests/test_seat_cooldown.py` already established the right pattern (`_with_store`: point both `$REVIEW_SEAT_COOLDOWN_FILE` and `$REVIEW_LOG_DIR` at a fresh temp dir, restore on teardown). The suites above never adopted it for the log-dir half.

## User impact

Every local `pytest` run silently writes real, unbounded log volume into the developer's actual log directory. On this machine that directory is currently 120,000+ files / 3.7GB. It also corrupts any `review stat` telemetry taken shortly after a test run — synthetic fixture text (fake auth/paywall bodies, fake model labels) gets mixed into real production call/retry logs and inflates failure-rate counts for whatever model the test fixtures happened to reuse (in this case, the real `claude:claude-fable-5` board entry).

## Cost of inaction

Continues to (a) bloat `~/Library/Logs/review-cli` without bound on every test run, and (b) silently poison any telemetry-based investigation (like review-cli#fable-seat-reliability, which had to specifically filter out test-fixture-shaped bodies — "boom0", "x", `example.com` URLs — to trust its own `review stat` output).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `tests/test_failover_pool.py`, `tests/test_provider_failover.py`, and `tests/test_board_deadline_wiring.py` isolate `$REVIEW_LOG_DIR` to a fresh temp dir per test (matching `tests/test_seat_cooldown.py::_with_store` or `tests/test_inseat_retry.py`'s existing fixture), with teardown restoring the prior value.
- [ ] A regression test (or a `conftest.py` audit script) confirms no test file that calls `write_retry_log`/`run_seat_with_retry`/`run_board_with_failover` can run without `$REVIEW_LOG_DIR` set to something other than the real `log_dir()`.

## What

`tests/test_run_stats.py::test_cli_default_board_run_records_roles_review_cli_221` and `tests/test_run_stats.py::test_cli_failover_backfill_records_actual_models_not_planned` both fail on a clean, unmodified checkout of `origin/main` (verified via `git stash` + rerun in a throwaway worktree while working on review-cli#fable-seat-reliability — these failures are NOT caused by that change and reproduce identically before and after it).

`test_cli_default_board_run_records_roles_review_cli_221` expects a real CLI board dispatch (all 4 pool seats forced to succeed via a stubbed `resolve_backend`) to record roles `{correctness, performance, quality, consistency}`, but gets `{security, performance, quality, consistency}` instead — `claude:claude-opus-4-8` (role `correctness`) is apparently missing from the dispatched pool, with `Qwen` (role `security`, priority #6 on the board) showing up instead. This looks like an unexpected startup-pool selection or availability-check discrepancy for `claude:claude-opus-4-8` specifically, independent of any Fable-related change.

`test_cli_failover_backfill_records_actual_models_not_planned` expects stderr to contain `"promoting reserve"` (the exact substring `panel.py:587` prints on a real mid-run backfill: `f"[review-cli] board: {result.model} failed — promoting reserve {promoted.display} ..."`) after forcing `claude:claude-fable-5` to fail — but the captured stderr never contains it, meaning the expected mid-run failover never actually fired in this test scenario.

## Why (motivation)

Both tests exercise the same reviewer-board dispatch/failover machinery (`_mode_review_board` / `select_pool_and_reserve_with_reuse` / `run_board_with_failover`) via the real CLI entrypoint. Something in that path currently behaves differently than these tests (and their own docstrings) expect, independent of board contents — this reproduces on the current `DEFAULT_BOARD` shape, not anything specific to the Fable reordering in review-cli#fable-seat-reliability.

## User impact

Anyone running the full `pytest` suite sees 2 failing tests unrelated to whatever they're actually working on, which erodes trust in "all green" as a real signal and makes a genuine regression in this exact area (startup pool selection / mid-run failover) harder to spot next to this known-broken baseline.

## Cost of inaction

The failing baseline stays red indefinitely; a future genuine regression in `_mode_review_board`'s pool/failover logic could hide behind these two already-broken tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root-cause why `claude:claude-opus-4-8` doesn't land in the startup pool in `test_cli_default_board_run_records_roles_review_cli_221`'s scenario (all seats stubbed available/successful) — is it a real selection bug, or a stale test expectation?
- [ ] Root-cause why the mid-run failover never prints "promoting reserve" in `test_cli_failover_backfill_records_actual_models_not_planned`'s scenario — is `run_board_with_failover` not detecting the forced Fable failure, or is the assertion stale?
- [ ] Both tests pass again (either by fixing the underlying dispatch code, or updating the test if its expectation was the stale part) on a clean `pytest` run.

## Skipped gates

- links: descriptive text (test names, function names, file:line), not repo/path references

comments.body:
Follow-up from the review-cli#fable-seat-reliability review gate (Codex and k3 both independently suggested "just fail Sol instead of Fable" as the fix for `test_cli_failover_backfill_records_actual_models_not_planned`). Tried it empirically rather than taking it on faith:

```python
resolver = _stub_resolve_backend({SOL_SEAT: 1})
r = _run_board_review_with_resolver(["--preset", "heavy"], resolver)
```

Result is NOT the expected "Codex backfills" — it's a different, more surprising failure:

```
[review-cli] board: Sol [consistency] failed — promoting reserve Qwen [security] (oc:commandcode/Qwen/Qwen3.7-Max)
models: ['commandcode:zai-org/GLM-5.2', 'oc:commandcode/moonshotai/Kimi-K2.7-Code', 'codex', 'oc:commandcode/Qwen/Qwen3.7-Max']
```

`claude:claude-opus-4-8` (which should be in the pool, and should be a genuine success since the stub returns rc=0 for every model except Sol) is completely MISSING from the recorded models, and the promoted reserve is Qwen (heavy-preset priority #6) instead of Codex (priority #5, the actual next-in-line reserve). This means the underlying `_mode_review_board` / `_chain_aware_available` / `provider_chain` machinery has a real bug independent of which specific seat is made to fail — it isn't just "the test picked Fable, which is no longer in the pool." Whoever picks this up should start by reproducing this exact scenario (fail Sol, not Fable) and tracing why Opus silently drops out and why the reserve promotion skips Codex.

Additional data point: across repeated full-suite runs during review-cli#fable-seat-reliability, `test_cli_default_board_run_records_roles_review_cli_221` was sometimes red and sometimes green with NO code changes in between (same worktree, same commit) -- consistent with the other finding posted above (Opus silently dropping out of a stubbed dispatch, Qwen promoted instead of the expected next-priority seat): this smells like a genuine race/nondeterminism in `_mode_review_board`'s pool-selection or dispatch path, not a simple stale assertion. Flagging so whoever picks this up doesn't assume a deterministic repro.

Update: `test_cli_failover_backfill_records_actual_models_not_planned` is now fixed and passing reliably (5/5 repeated runs) — my earlier report that the 'obvious fix' (fail Sol instead of Fable, expect Codex to backfill) didn't work was an artifact of a flawed manual reproduction script (a `sys.path`-manipulated standalone script that likely patched the wrong module instance, not the real pytest-collected one). Run through the actual test suite properly, targeting Sol as the failing seat with a full-set model comparison (not partial `in` checks) works correctly and stably.

`test_cli_default_board_run_records_roles_review_cli_221` (the other test mentioned above) is currently passing too in the latest full-suite run (2114 passed, 0 failed, 6 skipped) — consistent with the intermittent/flaky behavior already noted, not a fix. Leaving this issue open to track that flakiness, since it's a real, if intermittent, signal of something non-deterministic in the underlying pool-selection/dispatch path.

title: Fable seat: cooldown catches too few doomed dispatches + priority-1 wastes every review's first slot
body:
## What
Two compounding problems with the `claude:claude-fable-5` ("Fable") board seat:

1. `reviewlib/backends.py`'s `_chronic_unavailable_reason` (the function that decides whether `reviewlib.seat_cooldown.record_cooldown` should cache a dispatch as chronically doomed) only checks the "is currently unavailable" administrative-sentinel marker set on the `returncode == 0` branch. A real production retry-log (2026-06-26) shows Fable's CLI wrapper sometimes relays the IDENTICAL sentinel text with a NON-ZERO exit code — a shape the non-zero-exit branch never scans for (it only checks the separate session-limit/quota marker set). The cooldown cache never fires for that failure shape.
2. Independent of (1): `review stat` telemetry shows Fable's dispatch failure rate is 97.9-100% (chronic session/usage-limit exhaustion on the account it runs through), up from 67.7% two weeks earlier — and it sits at priority 1 in `reviewlib/config.py`'s `DEFAULT_BOARD` (and priority 3 in the operator's personal `~/.config/review-cli/config.yaml`, at `effort: xhigh`). Even with a perfect cooldown catch rate, priority 1 means a near-certain-doomed real dispatch burns first on every default review before a working seat ever answers.

## Why (motivation)
The cooldown cache (review-cli#185/#194, with escalation added in #221/#230) exists specifically to stop review-cli paying for a real dispatch to a seat already known to be chronically unavailable. Telemetry shows it is only catching a small fraction of Fable's doomed dispatches relative to how often it fails — this issue is where that gap gets root-caused and fixed.

## User impact
Every default `review diff` wastes wall-clock and token budget on a near-certain-failing Fable dispatch (at the most expensive `xhigh` effort tier in the operator's config) before a working seat ever produces a verdict — worse when the cooldown cache fails to catch a repeat of the exact same failure shape.

## Cost of inaction
Continues burning real dispatch cost (subprocess spawn + LLM round-trip) on a seat with a demonstrated ~100% failure rate, on every single review run, indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] `_chronic_unavailable_reason` recognizes the administrative-unavailable sentinel on BOTH the rc=0 and rc!=0 branches, with a regression test pinning the previously-uncaught non-zero-exit shape. — forced: code-only criterion (no UI/screenshot applicable); verified on merged main (d97452f): grep confirms both branches recognize _UNAVAILABLE_MARKERS in reviewlib/backends.py's _chronic_unavailable_reason, and 'python3 -m pytest tests/test_seat_cooldown.py::test_review_claude_records_cooldown_for_unavailable_sentinel_with_nonzero_exit -v' passes (1 passed)
- [x] Fable's board priority is demoted (code default + the operator's personal config) so it no longer occupies the routinely-dispatched pool, while remaining a last-resort reserve seat. — forced: code-only criterion (no UI/screenshot applicable); verified live: reviewlib/config.py's DEFAULT_BOARD has claude:claude-fable-5 at index 9 (last, priority 10), excluded from HEAVY_PRESET_BOARD; ~/.config/review-cli/config.yaml has claude:claude-fable-5 as the last entry in both models: and board:, with effort: medium (was xhigh) -- verified by reading the live file directly
- [x] Full test suite green (excluding any pre-existing, unrelated failures, documented separately). — forced: code-only criterion (no UI/screenshot applicable); 'python3 -m pytest -q' on merged main (d97452f) at 2026-08-29: 2174 passed, 6 skipped, 0 failed, in 379.65s

title: dashboard/spec-web autostart hardcodes /usr/bin/env, absent on NixOS
body:
\`reviewlib/dashboard/service.py:_env_clear_prefix()\` (reused by \`specweb/service.py\`) hardcodes \`/usr/bin/env\` as the argv prefix that clears \`$REVIEW_CLI_ACTIVE\` before spawning the managed dashboard/spec-web \`__serve\` child (review-cli#180, PR #279).

This is deliberate — the alternative (\`shutil.which("env")\`, a caller-controlled PATH lookup) reopens a real PATH-injection security hole that a hardcoded absolute path closes (see PR #279's own review history, codex P1/P2). But the hardcoded path assumes \`/usr/bin/env\` exists, which is NOT guaranteed on every POSIX host — notably NixOS (and some minimal containers), where it's normally absent.

**Impact**: on such a host, \`review dashboard start\`/\`enable\` (and the spec-web equivalent) fails loudly at spawn (ENOENT / systemd \`203/EXEC\`) rather than launching the managed server.

**Status as landed**: treated as an accepted, documented tradeoff for now — 3 of 4 independent review passes on PR #279 examined this exact scenario and ruled it non-blocking (fails loud, not silent; consistent with the pre-existing \`shutil.which("review")\` pattern in the same module that has the same class of exposure). One review pass (codex) rated it P1.

**Real fix** likely needs \`agenttools_service\` (the shared \`agenttools-tools\` service-manager lib this module builds on) to support an \`env=\` override on \`Service\`/\`ServiceManager\`, so the guard var can be cleared via subprocess \`env=\` instead of an \`env -u\` argv wrapper — removing the need to resolve any \`env\` binary at all. That's cross-repo scope, deliberately not done in PR #279.

title: dashboard _fallback_seat_for ignores active preset — now shows Fable as GLM's fallback in both presets
body:
## What

`reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py`'s `_fallback_seat_for` (used by the dashboard's Errors-tab fallback hint) always derives "the next seat after a failing one" from the RAW `DEFAULT_BOARD` priority order — it has no concept of which PRESET (`default`/`heavy`/`light`) or custom `board:` was actually active for a given run.

Since review-cli#fable-seat-reliability demoted Fable to `DEFAULT_BOARD`'s last position, this now means: for GLM (`oc:zai/glm-5.2`), the raw-board fallback hint is Fable — but Fable is excluded from BOTH `DEFAULT_PRESET_BOARD` and `HEAVY_PRESET_BOARD` (a confirmed ~100% dispatch failure rate). So for either built-in preset, GLM failing is actually the LAST seat with no real fallback, but the dashboard tells the user "Fable" — a seat that preset would never actually dispatch.

## Why (motivation)

This is a pre-existing architectural limitation (raw-board-only fallback derivation, no preset awareness) that predates review-cli#fable-seat-reliability — before that change, the identical imprecision already existed for the mirror case (Fable failing showed Sol as its "fallback," even though Sol is also excluded from the default preset). The Fable/Sol demotion didn't introduce the underlying bug, it just relocated which seat's fallback hint is now wrong.

## User impact

A developer using the dashboard's Errors tab to understand "what happened after seat X failed" sees an incorrect next-seat hint for whichever preset/board was actually active, whenever the failing seat's true next-in-preset seat differs from its next-in-raw-board seat (currently: GLM in the default/heavy presets).

## Cost of inaction

The dashboard keeps giving a plausible-looking but wrong fallback hint for this specific case (and any future board reordering that creates the same raw-vs-preset divergence).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_fallback_seat_for` (or a preset-aware variant) computes the fallback from the ACTUALLY-ACTIVE board/preset when that context is available to the caller, falling back to the raw-board chain (today's behavior) only when preset context is genuinely unknown.
- [ ] A regression test pins that GLM's fallback hint under the `default`/`heavy` presets is "no fallback" (or the correct preset-specific next seat), not Fable.

title: seat_cooldown: chronic quota exhaustion delivered as HTTP 429 (API transport) is never cached
body:
## What

`reviewlib/backends.py`'s `_chronic_unavailable_reason` (the function that decides whether `reviewlib.seat_cooldown` caches a dispatch as chronically doomed) has a `_looks_transient` guard that withholds the cache for any rc!=0 response whose status/wording overlaps with retry.py's transient vocabulary — this was added in review-cli#fable-seat-reliability specifically to stop a real 503/529 gateway blip from being mis-cached as an hours-long chronic cooldown.

The trade-off (k3 review finding, round 8 of that same PR's review gate): Anthropic's API signals BOTH a brief rate-limit spike AND genuine account-level usage/session-limit exhaustion via the same HTTP 429 status. So on the API transport (`REVIEW_CLAUDE_MODE=api`, `review_claude_api`'s `HTTPError` path sets `returncode = exc.code`), a genuinely CHRONIC quota-exhaustion failure carrying "session limit"-style text now ALSO gets withheld from the cache, because `_looks_transient` sees `returncode=429` and returns True before the quota-marker check ever runs.

This mirrors `retry.classify_failure` exactly (retry.py's own `_SEAT_FATAL_PATTERNS` only recognises the word "quota", not "session limit", so retry.py itself would also call this RETRYABLE) — so it is not a divergence bug, but it does mean the cooldown cache's whole point (stop paying for a real dispatch to a KNOWN-doomed seat) doesn't fire for this specific delivery shape.

## Why (motivation)

The confirmed-live production evidence for Fable's failures (a real 2026-06-26 log) is a plain CLI-transport exit code (`exit=1`), not an API-transport 429 — so this gap is currently theoretical for Fable specifically. But any seat that DOES run via the API transport (`REVIEW_CLAUDE_MODE=api`) and hits genuine chronic quota exhaustion would be affected.

## User impact

On the API transport specifically, a seat with genuine chronic quota exhaustion pays a full real dispatch (plus in-seat retry budget, since retry.py itself also treats 429 as retryable) on every single review invocation, indefinitely — the cooldown cache never engages.

## Cost of inaction

Continues costing real dispatch + retry-budget wall-clock/tokens for any seat that hits this specific failure shape (429 + chronic quota text), with no cross-process caching to stop it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gather real telemetry on whether any seat's real failures actually arrive as 429 + `_CHRONIC_QUOTA_MARKERS` text (via `review stat` or direct log inspection) before deciding the fix — the two candidate fixes (exempt quota markers from the transient guard entirely, vs. check quota markers before the transient guard only when the numeric status is 429 specifically) have different false-positive risk profiles the confirmed-live data should decide between.
- [ ] Whichever fix is chosen, a regression test pins BOTH directions: the primary confirmed-live shape from review-cli#fable-seat-reliability (`rc=503, stderr="session limit reached; service unavailable"` → NOT cached, a real transient blip) and the new target shape (`rc=429, stderr="...session limit..."` with no other transient wording → cached, genuine chronic exhaustion).

title: preset_pool_size(None)/load_board({}) don't derive from DEFAULT_PRESET (unlike preset_board(None))
body:
Found during review of #305 (rounds default 3 / incremental brainstorm grounding / DEFAULT_PRESET=light), by two independent reviewers across two review rounds. Deliberately NOT fixed in #305 -- see reasoning below.

**The gap:** `preset_board(None)` (reviewlib/config.py) already resolves via `PRESET_BOARDS[DEFAULT_PRESET]`, so it correctly tracks whatever `DEFAULT_PRESET` is set to. Two sibling functions do NOT:
- `preset_pool_size(None)` still returns the separate `DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE` constant (4), not `PRESET_POOL_SIZES[DEFAULT_PRESET]`.
- `load_board({})` (an absent/empty `board:`, `preset=None`) falls back to `list(DEFAULT_PRESET_BOARD)` directly -- high effort, not whatever `DEFAULT_PRESET` currently points to.

A direct library/MCP caller composing `preset_board(None)` + `preset_pool_size(None)` now gets a mismatched pair: the light board (2 seats, medium effort) sized to 4. `load_board({})`'s callers get the OLD default board's effort even though `DEFAULT_PRESET` says light.

**Why not fixed in #305:** I traced every real CLI call site (`cli.py`'s `active_preset`/`effective_pool_size` resolution, `_show_board`, the pool guard) and confirmed NONE of them actually hit the `None`-fallback branch of `preset_pool_size`/`load_board` in the bare-invocation case -- `active_preset` is always resolved to a real preset name (or explicitly `None` for a genuinely custom `board:`) before either function is called. I attempted a fix to `preset_pool_size(None)` and reverted it: that same `None` branch is ALSO what a custom-config-board-with-no-`pool:`-key falls back to, and changing it would silently drop such a user from pool 4 to pool 2 -- a real behavior change for an established custom-board user, which is a DIFFERENT (and arguably wrong) thing to bundle into 'make the bare default cheaper.'

**What actually needs to happen:** a coordinated pass across `preset_board`, `preset_pool_size`, and `load_board` that explicitly defines what `None`/absent-preset means in EACH context ("the preset system's own default" vs "no preset in play, using a raw custom board") -- they currently conflate two different callers under one signature. Needs real test coverage for the custom-board-no-pool-key case specifically, so a fix doesn't silently change behavior for existing custom-board users the way my first attempt would have.

Also worth folding in while touching this area (Low priority, found same session):
- `tests/test_run_stats.py`: `_run_board_review_and_get_record` and `_run_board_review_with_resolver` are ~90% duplicated (same stubbing/isolation dance); the `REVIEW_SEAT_COOLDOWN_FILE" save/restore boilerplate is now hand-copied 4x across this file. A `@contextmanager` helper would remove the duplication and the class of restore-bug it invites (pop vs reassign).
- `reviewlib/sessions.py`: `path.name[: -len(_LOG_SUFFIX)] if path.name.endswith(_LOG_SUFFIX) else path.stem` is duplicated 3x (`_derive_id`, `_parse_timestamp`, `find_session`) with inconsistent formatting between copies. Extract `_log_stem(path: Path) -> str`.

comments.body:
Additional findings from the same review series (round 5, GLM quality pass) worth folding into whatever fixes this:

- The guard fix (`preset_pool_size(active_preset)` at cli.py's two `_evaluate_pool_or_bail` call sites) now needs 4 separate comments to defend the deliberate `preset_board(None)` vs `preset_pool_size(None)` asymmetry. Cleaner fix: name the concept — add `config_roster_default_pool() -> int` (returns `DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE`), use it at the guard sites and the main dispatch resolution (cli.py ~4211-4218), and let `preset_pool_size(None)` either track `preset_board` or reject `None` outright. Then the defensive comments (including the new test assertion in `test_package_facade_exports_preset_surface`) can go away.
- The guard's `default_pool` expression is duplicated verbatim at both call sites (cli.py ~4918, ~4997); the ACTUAL dispatch resolution (~4211-4218) is a third, slightly different encoding of the same precedence, and already disagrees in one corner (explicit `--preset X` + config `pool: N` — dispatch takes the preset's pool, the guard's proposal text takes the config pool). Harmless today (only affects proposal TEXT, not real dispatch), but worth a single `resolve_default_pool(args, config, active_preset)` helper shared by both.
- `reviewlib/modes/review.py:187,1127` and `cli.py`'s `_show_board` signature default still default `pool_size` to `DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE` (4) — dead today (the CLI always passes explicitly) but a live trap for the future MCP seam AGENTS.md reserves this layer for: a direct `mode_review(..., board=<light board>)` call omitting `pool_size` would run 4 seats against a 2-seat board.
- Test env-isolation boilerplate (`REVIEW_SEAT_COOLDOWN_FILE` save/set/restore) is now hand-copied 6x in `test_run_stats.py` alone, 10+ repo-wide. Same file also has an adjacent bug: `os.environ.pop("REVIEW_LOG_DIR", None)` in the `finally` unconditionally deletes an outer `REVIEW_LOG_DIR` instead of save/restoring it like the cooldown var right next to it — a caller running with `REVIEW_LOG_DIR` already set in its own environment loses it after the first board test in-process.
- `brainstorm.py`'s `--max-rounds` help says "hard cap" but a sub-floor value (e.g. `--rounds 1 --max-rounds 2`) is silently inflated to the 3-round floor. Pre-existing (was inflated to 5 before this change), just newly visible since the floor line was touched.

None of these block correctness (2 of 3 round-5 reviewers returned a clean verdict) — filing here rather than blocking the rounds/brainstorm/light-preset change (review-cli#305) any further.

title: opencode true-silence cooldown clear uses stale bare rc=0 check, diverges from claude path (backends.py _record_true_silence_if_needed)
body:
## Summary

Found by a 3-model \`review diff\` pass (Opus, Codex, GLM — independently, same root cause) while landing an unrelated PR's merge-with-main. Pre-existing on `main` as of #303 (`d97452f`, "catch chronic rc!=0/seat-fatal failures + demote Fable") — not introduced by that PR's own diff, so filing separately rather than blocking on it.

## The bug

`reviewlib/backends.py`, `_record_true_silence_if_needed` (opencode path), final branch:

```python
reason = _chronic_unavailable_reason(proc)
if reason is not None:
    record_cooldown(model, reason)
elif proc.returncode == 0 and proc.stdout.strip():
    clear_cooldown(model)
```

`#303` upgraded the two `claude` call sites (`review_claude`, `review_with_images`) from this exact bare `returncode == 0 and stdout.strip()` pattern to `_clears_cooldown_history(result)` → `result_is_usable(result)`, specifically to stop clearing history for the rc=0 "unavailable" sentinel exception that same PR added. The opencode call site (`_record_true_silence_if_needed`) was left on the old bare pattern.

## Concrete failure scenario

1. An `oc:*` seat accrues true-silence/chronic trips, leaving an *expired* cooldown with a retained `fail_count` (escalation history).
2. A new dispatch returns `returncode=0`, a short sentinel stdout (e.g. `"GLM-5.2 is currently unavailable"`), and stderr that looks transient (e.g. `"upstream HTTP 503 while proxying"`).
3. `_chronic_unavailable_reason(proc)` correctly returns `None` for this shape (it withholds caching when stderr is transient).
4. The opencode branch then falls into `elif proc.returncode == 0 and proc.stdout.strip():` → `stdout.strip()` is truthy → `clear_cooldown` wipes the escalation history.

Result: the still-unavailable seat's cooldown escalation resets to zero; the next real chronic failure restarts at the shortest cooldown window instead of escalating from where it left off — the same "never actually escalates" class of regression #303 fixed for the `claude` path, now reproduced on the `opencode` path.

The `claude` path already has a regression test for the equivalent shape (`test_wiring_review_claude_rc0_transient_stderr_sentinel_does_not_clear_cooldown`); `test_true_silence_then_rc0_quota_body_then_true_silence_preserves_escalation` covers a sentinel *without* stderr (records via the chronic branch), so it never reaches the buggy `elif`.

## Suggested fix

`elif _clears_cooldown_history(proc): clear_cooldown(model)` — `result_is_usable` only touches `.returncode`/`.stdout`, so a `subprocess.CompletedProcess` duck-types fine. Add the missing opencode-side sibling test mirroring the claude-side one.

## Provenance

- Found independently by 3 models (Opus/correctness, Codex/consistency, GLM/quality) in one `review diff` pass against a routine main-merge diff.
- Confirmed via \`git log -1 -- reviewlib/backends.py\` on both the PR branch and \`origin/main\`: both point at \`d97452f\` (#303) — this is pre-existing on \`main\`, not something PR #278 touches or introduces.

title: call_log_cache: low-severity quality follow-ups from review-cli#317 review
body:
Non-blocking quality items from the round-3 review of #317's call-log cache (reviewlib/dashboard/call_log_cache.py), deliberately deferred rather than blocking the P0-adjacent stat/dashboard perf fix further:

1. Rename `save()` -> `prune_deleted()` (or similar) — under autocommit, writes are already persisted when they happen; `save()` only prunes, and the current name reads like a required flush.
2. Document (README/AGENTS.md) that the cache adds roughly 1x extra on-disk size to $REVIEW_LOG_DIR (full call bodies, JSON), and consider a `REVIEW_DISABLE_CALL_LOG_CACHE=1` opt-out plus an eviction/size cap.
3. `save()` does a full directory glob + full table scan every call — cheap relative to parsing, but worth reconciling with the module's own 'never loads what it doesn't need' framing, e.g. prune every Nth scan instead of every scan.
4. `save()` reads the `_connections` dict without taking `_lock` (unlike `_conn_for`) — safe today (GIL-atomic dict ops) but inconsistent locking discipline.
5. The 'call-log files are write-once' rationale comment is duplicated near-verbatim at both `parser.py` and `tokenstats.py` call sites — collapse to a one-line pointer at each site, full rationale stays in the module docstring.
6. `get_or_parse(directory, path, parse)` takes both `directory` and `path` with nothing enforcing `path.parent == directory` — consider deriving `directory` from `path.parent` or asserting the relationship in debug builds.
7. Test nit: `_serialize` iterates a `set` of field names, so JSON key order is nondeterministic row-to-row — sort for byte-stable, diffable cache rows.
8. `server.py`'s `_emit_activity` still calls `parser.parse_call_log` directly (uncached) — not a bug (it only ever sees just-changed files, a cache miss anyway), but routing it through `get_or_parse` would give one consistent parse discipline across the whole module.

comments.body:
Additional low-severity items from round-4 review, also deferred:

9. `_deserialize` validates the key SET but not value TYPES — a right-keys/wrong-types row (e.g. `body` is a dict instead of str) is constructed into a CallLog and crashes downstream on first real use, and persists forever since (mtime,size) never change again for a finished log. Add isinstance guards per field before constructing.
10. One corrupt db file permanently disables the cache for every future process with zero surfaced signal — no self-heal, no diagnostic. On `sqlite3.DatabaseError` specifically, consider best-effort unlink + one retry before memoizing failure as permanent; don't memoize transient `OperationalError` (EMFILE, momentary read-only mount) as failure either.
11. `CallLog.path` can go stale after a metadata-preserving copy/move of the log dir (cosmetic only — it's a display field, nothing re-opens the file by that path). Worth a doc line.
12. Test hygiene: the must-not-reparse lambda hack in one test should be a named function; every dashboard test that touches the cache leaves an open sqlite connection in the module-global `_connections` for the process lifetime (bounded, but a `close()`/`close_all()` API + teardown use would be cleaner).

13. `CallLog.path` (returned on a cache hit) goes stale forever if the log directory is ever moved/renamed — a finished log's (mtime,size) never change, so nothing invalidates the row. Cosmetic only (nothing re-opens a file by this path; it's display-only). One-line fix if ever prioritized: reconstruct `path` from the current (directory, filename) on every hit rather than trusting the stored value. (review-cli#317 review round 5, k3 finding 2 — a first attempt at this fix broke several existing tests' exact-equality assertions and was reverted rather than chase that further.)

14. round-6 review flagged: a transiently-unreadable file (e.g. network-mounted $REVIEW_LOG_DIR hitting EIO/EACCES mid-read) gets permanently cached as an empty-body CallLog once — pre-diff behavior self-healed on the next scan since there was no persistent cache; now it doesn't until `_PARSER_VERSION` is bumped. Requires an unusual deployment (network FS); deferred rather than modifying parser.py's read-failure contract to fix cleanly.
15. No dedicated regression test for the non-UTF-8-filename crash fix (widened SELECT/INSERT except clauses to catch ValueError alongside sqlite3.Error, round 6 k3 finding 1) — the code fix is in, a test proving it specifically would be good defense-in-depth.

16. `_CACHE_ERRORS` tuple is a per-call local inside `get_or_parse`, not shared with `save()` (which only catches `sqlite3.Error`) — hoist to a module constant.
17. Redundant `directory` parameter on `get_or_parse(directory, path, parse)` — always `path.parent` at both call sites; could derive it internally instead of trusting callers to pass a matching value.
18. `_deserialize` still only type-checks datetime fields (via the fix in this PR) — non-datetime fields (round, body, etc.) aren't validated, so a crafted db row with right keys/wrong types (e.g. `body: 123`) would construct successfully and crash downstream instead of being caught as a cache miss. Requires write access to the 0700 log dir already (no privilege gain), so low severity.
19. Test coverage gaps: no test for a transient (vs permanent) connect failure recovering; no integration test running the real `parse_call_log` through the cache end-to-end (all tests use fake parse callables).
20. `tokenstats.py`'s local `from .parser import parse_call_log" import (inside `list_call_logs`) is now stale/redundant — the module already imports from `.parser` at top level; this diff touched the function, so it's a free one-line cleanup if anyone's back in that file.

21. Design tension flagged round 8: `_serialize`'s deliberate raise-on-non-serializable-field (added round 2 to avoid silently masking a bug) means a future incompatible `CallLog` field type breaks EVERY `load_sessions`/`list_call_logs` call outright, which conflicts with `tokenstats.py`'s own documented 'never raises' contract for report-only tooling. Suggested resolution if prioritized: catch `TypeError` at the `get_or_parse` call sites, log once, and flip a process-wide cache-disabled flag (loud-but-non-fatal) rather than the current 'crash everything' or the rejected 'silently swallow forever' extremes.
22. `save()`'s full glob + full table SELECT runs on every scan (not just when something changed), under the per-directory lock — cheap relative to parsing but worth time-gating (track last-prune monotonic time) if this ever shows up as real contention.
23. Positional row indexing (`row[0]`/`row[1]`/etc.) instead of `conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row" + named access.

24. `save()`'s new pre-existing-db-open path: the comment on the early-return branch says 'no connection opened this process' but that's only true for the never-attempted case, not the memoized-connect-failure case — both hit `_connections.get() is None`. Cosmetic/readability only (both cases return correctly either way).
25. Same branch has a TOCTOU between `Path.exists()` and `sqlite3.connect()`: if the db is deleted in that window, connect recreates an empty db despite the comment saying 'never CREATE'. Benign (empty db, no privacy leak, no rows to protect) since nothing in-repo deletes this file — flagged LOW by both reviewers.

title: Interactive cross-account usage/cost stats dashboard (tokens, $, wasted spend on failed runs)
body:
## What
Build an interactive, self-hosted dashboard giving Alex a full picture of Claude usage across all 3 personal claude-rotate accounts (and the pre-rotation ~/.claude default identity): weekly/monthly token and hypothetical-API-dollar breakdowns, sliceable by role (main-thread vs subagent/sidechain), model, task, project, harness (Claude Code, codex, opencode/oc, Oh-My-Pi/omp), and provider/vendor -- plus a first-class 'wasted spend' metric that isolates cost burned on runs that failed/wedged without producing a working result (the concrete motivating case: review-cli's 'fable' board seat, documented at review-cli README ~line 1368 as '4,322 of 6,383 recorded runs dispatched Fable and it failed', tracked review-cli#fable-seat-reliability, already demoted to last-resort reserve in every preset because of this).

## Why (motivation)
Alex asked directly for visibility into what his Claude usage actually costs (in real per-token API-price terms, since these are subscription accounts with no native per-token billing) split every way he cares about, specifically calling out that Grafana is too heavy for this and that he wants something genuinely interactive (ad-hoc pivoting), plus specifically wants to quantify how much was burned on the fable seat's known high failure rate.

## User impact
Alex gets a real answer to 'what is my Claude usage actually costing me and where is it being wasted' instead of guessing -- both for personal capacity planning across 3 rotating accounts and for catching future seats/harnesses that silently burn spend while failing, the way fable did.

## Cost of inaction
Usage keeps accumulating (3.2GB+ of session history already sitting in ~/.claude/projects alone, unaggregated) with no visibility; a repeat of the fable pattern (a broken seat quietly consuming real tokens run after run before anyone notices the failure rate) goes undetected in any other harness/model/seat until someone happens to read raw logs by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Ingests real per-message usage (input/output/cache tokens, model, timestamp, project cwd, isSidechain-derived role) from every CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR session-log tree (~/.claude/projects plus each ~/.claude-accounts/account-N/projects), not just review-cli's own call logs
- [ ] Also ingests review-cli's own per-call log store (log_dir()) for the harnesses/providers review-cli itself drives (opencode, Oh-My-Pi, codex, claude-subprocess, plus REST backends that DO carry real usage+cost per review-cli README ~line 660) -- two distinct data sources, both required, documented as such in the spec
- [ ] Computes a hypothetical USD cost per record using published Anthropic API list pricing per model, clearly labeled as an estimate since these are subscription not pay-per-token accounts
- [ ] Supports weekly and monthly rollups plus true ad-hoc interactive pivoting/filtering across role, model, task, project, harness, and provider dimensions simultaneously (not a fixed set of static charts)
- [ ] Ships a first-class wasted-spend / failed-run-cost breakdown that can isolate and total cost attributable to runs that errored or wedged without a working result, grounded in and validated against the known fable-seat failure pattern as a concrete test case
- [ ] Framework/architecture decision is documented with real tradeoffs (this investigation recommends DuckDB for local aggregation plus FINOS Perspective, a WASM MIT-licensed pivot engine, embedded in review-cli's existing stdlib-HTTP plus vanilla-JS dashboard SPA for genuine client-side pivoting, matching the ecosystem's established no-heavy-extra-services taste; Metabase noted as a heavier but more turnkey GUI-BI fallback if the custom-integration path proves too costly) -- Grafana explicitly ruled out per Alex's own ask
- [ ] A phased plan exists distinguishing a realistic first cut from the full everything-explorable vision, since this is genuinely large scope
- [ ] Notes the Haft v7 spec-methodology investigation performed for this ticket: haft init plus haft spec onboard were run live against review-cli and confirmed working (project id qnt_57872bb8), but Haft's onboarding is a whole-repository target and enabling spec process requiring Alex's own interactive answers at every phase before any feature-level DecisionRecord or WorkCommission can exist -- it was NOT completed or faked in this pass; the acceptance criteria and content in this ticket are the spec substance for now, and a full Haft spine remains a separate, explicitly-scoped follow-up if Alex wants to invest that interactive time

title: review dashboard status reports stale default port (7878) instead of the actual bound port after --port override
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
[reviewlib/cli.py](file:///Users/ultra/xp/review-cli/reviewlib/cli.py)'s _dashboard_subcommand parses --port fresh on every invocation (argparse default=DEFAULT_DASHBOARD_PORT=7878) and builds a NEW Service descriptor from that value every time. [dashboard_service()](file:///Users/ultra/xp/review-cli/reviewlib/dashboard/service.py) keys the underlying agenttools_service.Service by name='dashboard' only, so the shared service lib's pidfile lookup DOES find the right running process regardless of which port was just parsed -- but the status text's displayed port/URL is echoed from the freshly-parsed (default) Service.port, not from what the actual running process is bound to. So start correctly binds the requested port, but any later status/stop call that omits --port silently displays the wrong port for the SAME correctly-found process.

## User impact
Reproduced live: 'review dashboard --port 8799 start' bound and served correctly (curl http://127.0.0.1:8799/ -> 200), but 'review dashboard status' (no --port) printed 'dashboard: running (pid 97989) -- http://127.0.0.1:7878' -- same pid, wrong URL. Anyone who starts the dashboard on a non-default port and later checks status (a likely flow -- e.g. running it as part of the usage-stats dashboard work in [review-cli#321](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/321)) gets a URL that doesn't work, with no indication anything is wrong.

## Cost of inaction
Every future non-default-port dashboard run keeps reporting a dead/wrong URL from status, quietly training users to distrust or ignore review dashboard status output.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] review dashboard --port <N> start followed by review dashboard status (no --port) reports the actually-bound port <N>, not the hardcoded DEFAULT_DASHBOARD_PORT (7878)
- [ ] the URL printed by status is genuinely dialable -- curl against it succeeds -- for a dashboard started on a non-default port

title: review dashboard /api/stats never returns on a large log_dir() -- reproduced: >150s, 0 bytes, on 10GB / 130,668 files
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Reproduced live on this machine: log_dir() (from reviewlib/process, currently /Users/ultra/Library/Logs/review-cli) holds 10GB across 130,668 files. 'curl -m 150 http://127.0.0.1:8799/api/stats' returned curl error 28 (operation timed out) after 150.07s with 0 bytes received -- the endpoint had not produced any response at all in that window. [reviewlib/dashboard/server.py](file:///Users/ultra/xp/review-cli/reviewlib/dashboard/server.py) memoizes /api/stats against a log_dir() fingerprint (see _cached_stats / _log_dir_fingerprint), so the FIRST request after any log_dir() change pays a full synchronous rescan+parse of every file before the memoized cache can help -- and at 130k+ files that rescan does not complete in a reasonable time at all.

## User impact
The dashboard's own /api/stats aggregate is unusable on any real, long-lived install once log_dir() accumulates enough history -- this machine got there after normal day-to-day usage, not an artificial stress case. It is also a direct blocker for [review-cli#321](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/321) (the new cross-account usage/cost stats dashboard), which needs exactly this kind of large-scale log aggregation to work reliably -- if the existing, narrower /api/stats already can't finish a scan at this size, the broader effort will hit the same wall.

## Cost of inaction
review dashboard stays effectively broken for its core stats view on any machine with real usage history, and the cross-account stats work inherits the same unscalable aggregation approach instead of being designed around the actual bottleneck from day one.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] GET /api/stats responds within a bounded, documented time budget (e.g. under 10s) even when log_dir() holds 100k+ files / 10GB+, via incremental/cached aggregation instead of a synchronous full-directory rescan per request
- [ ] the fix is validated against a log_dir() of a comparable real size (10GB+ / 100k+ files), not just a small fixture directory, since the bug only manifests at this scale

title: dashboard: loading the full ~10GB call-log directory (about 132k files) balloons the process to 32.8GB RSS and can thrash the machine
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
CallLog keeps the full streamed body text in memory for every one of roughly 132000 calls, all needed at once for the aggregate stats/list view. On this real install that balloons the dashboard process to 32.8GB RSS, confirmed via a live process memory sample, causing severe machine-wide memory pressure and swapping -- unrelated parts of the system became unresponsive while the process held that much RAM.

## User impact
the dashboard cannot be safely re-enabled at this install's real data volume without OOM/thrashing risk; it is currently intentionally stopped as a stopgap

## Cost of inaction
the dashboard stays permanently disabled, or gets re-enabled and repeatedly OOMs/thrashes the machine again next time someone turns it back on without knowing about this limit

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] review-cli dashboard process stays under a documented safe memory ceiling when serving /api/stats against a real, large log directory — forced: Live proof, not a visual UI feature: restarted the launchd-managed dashboard (com.ultra.review-dashboard, PID 16176) against the real ~134,628-file/17GB log directory post-fix (PR #336, review-cli#326). GET /api/stats returned real aggregate data (call_count=101247, session_count=9052, success_rate=0.5871) in 1.4-2.9s. RSS sampled via 'ps -p 16176 -o rss' throughout the cold-cache full re-parse (forced by the _PARSER_VERSION 1->2 bump): peaked around 1.3-1.7GB (6.7% of a 24GB machine), never approached the prior 32.8GB incident. Confirmed stable (not still climbing) across repeated samples over several minutes.
- [x] [CallLog](file:///Users/ultra/xp/review-cli/reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py) no longer holds full body text in memory for the aggregate/list view, only fetching it on-demand for a single session's detail view — forced: Verified in code + tests, not a visual feature: CallLog.body/stderr_lines are now capped at parse time (_cap_body/_cap_stderr_lines, reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py), so the in-memory/session-cache representation of every call is bounded (~16KB max per body) instead of holding the full streamed text. Classification (completed/has_error/is_paywall/etc.) is computed once from the FULL text before capping and stored, so the aggregate/list view's health classification stays correct despite the cap. Live RSS proof (criterion 1) confirms the aggregate view no longer holds full body text: 1.68GB RSS for 101,247 calls vs the prior 32.8GB for a comparable/smaller working set.

title: dashboard: body-derived diagnostic markers (skill_md/memory_md/diff counts) can be lost to body truncation
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
review-cli#326 fixed a 32.8GB dashboard memory balloon by capping retained CallLog body and stderr text (see [reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py](reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py)). Round 2 review already fixed the correctness-critical classification fields by computing them once on the full untruncated text during parsing. top_oversized_calls was deliberately left reading the now-capped body, since it is a diagnostic report, not a health classifier.

## User impact
top_oversized_calls picks exactly the largest calls by size -- the calls most likely to exceed the cap and most likely to carry real diff or memory content -- so this report is the one most exposed to the gap. An operator investigating an oversized call could see a zero diff-file count for a call that actually embeds a huge diff, just because the marker landed in the truncated middle.

## Cost of inaction
Low severity: this endpoint is diagnostic only, not a health or success-rate metric, and the ranking key itself is unaffected -- but it stays a known, silent accuracy gap in exactly the report an operator reaches for to investigate the biggest calls.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] top_oversized_calls in [reviewlib/dashboard/tokenstats.py](reviewlib/dashboard/tokenstats.py) computes its diff-git, binary-stub, skill-md, and memory-md markers from the FULL on-disk log body, not the capped in-memory CallLog.body, for calls whose size_bytes exceeds CALL_BODY_STORE_CAP.
- [ ] Add a regression test with an on-disk log larger than the cap whose only diff-git marker sits in the truncated-away middle, asserting the marker count is still correct.
- [ ] compute_harness_stats in [reviewlib/dashboard/tokenstats.py](reviewlib/dashboard/tokenstats.py) (skill_md_calls/memory_md_calls, ~line 433) and top_oversized_calls (~line 662) both check for SKILL.md/MEMORY.md/diff-git/binary-stub markers in call.body, which review-cli#326 now caps to CALL_BODY_STORE_CAP; a marker in the omitted middle of a huge log is silently missed on BOTH call sites, not just the oversized-calls report -- compute_harness_stats feeds the main per-harness stats table shown in every review stat run, so this is a more visible gap than initially scoped.

## What


## Why (motivation)
Found while restarting the dashboard for review-cli#326: the HAND-CREATED ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.ultra.review-dashboard.plist in actual use had a minimal PATH (no ~/.files/bin), so its self-spawned __serve subprocess fell through _review_argv0()'s 'sys.executable -m reviewlib' fallback -- which fails on THIS machine's dev-symlink install (reviewlib isn't pip-installed, so -m reviewlib finds nothing). The next time someone runs review dashboard enable (or the plist is regenerated/reset) on this or a similarly-configured dev-symlink machine, the dashboard silently fails to start again, and whoever hits it has to re-derive this same PATH root cause from scratch.

- [ ] Reproduce: on a machine where review-cli is installed via the legacy symlink path (install.sh, no pip/pipx), start the dashboard as a launchd LaunchAgent with a minimal EnvironmentVariables.PATH (no dir containing the review symlink). title: Session-detail view: stderr-only rendering, missing round grouping, missing roles/prompts
body:
## What
Three related session-detail rendering gaps found while investigating owner-reported bugs on sess-20260901T142348_781521 and sess-20260901T155805_494707: (1) a call's real stdout verdict was buried/indistinguishable inside a wall of stderr-tagged transcript lines (codex genuinely streams its whole transcript, including its own echo of the prompt, to real OS stderr — the capture itself is correct, but the UI gave the stdout verdict no visual priority); (2) the Calls list never grouped by round even when a session (brainstorm/quorum) carries multiple real rounds; (3) a call's board role (e.g. correctness/consistency) and its prompt (when a subprocess backend echoes it back into its own transcript) were never surfaced at all outside brainstorm personas.

## Why (motivation)
Alex (dashboard owner) reported all three while actively browsing session detail: 'и все почему-то в stderr, даже diff', 'надо группировать по заголовкам раунды', 'почему-то роли моделей не пишутся / они что без ролей?', 'где промпты?'

## User impact
The dashboard's session-detail view is unusable for actually understanding what a call did: a successful review reads as an unbroken wall of red/amber 'error' styled stderr, multi-round brainstorms are an undifferentiated flat list, and there is no way to see which lens a seat reviewed under or what was actually asked.

## Cost of inaction
The owner keeps misreading healthy calls as broken (stderr noise), can't audit round-by-round brainstorm progress, and can't verify a seat's role/prompt assignment from the dashboard at all.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Session-detail shows a clearly-labeled 'Result (stdout)' block for a call's real output, separate from a collapsible 'verbose transcript (stderr, N lines)' section (auto-expanded only when the call errored or produced no stdout).
- [ ] Session-detail groups the Calls list under 'Round N' headers when a session has more than one distinct round (e.g. a multi-round brainstorm); a single-round session (the common diff-review case) still renders flat, never a fabricated 'Round 0' header.
- [ ] Each call in session-detail shows its board role/lens (e.g. correctness, consistency) when the model resolves to a known board seat.
- [ ] Each call shows its recovered prompt when a subprocess backend (codex/claude CLI) echoed it into its own transcript, or an explicit 'no prompt recovered' note when it did not (REST backends never carry one, by design).

title: Dashboard board-lens views ignore per-repo custom board config and rewrite history
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Two independent reviewers (Codex, Fable) flagged this during review of the Stats-view redesign (review-cli#343): reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py's compute_stats() builds by_dimension from _board_models(), which always reads the static DEFAULT_BOARD constant in reviewlib/config.py, never the user's actual configured board (config.yaml board: key, read elsewhere via load_board()). This is a pre-existing characteristic of _board_models() already shared by the Models and roles tab and the Errors tab fallback hint, not something new -- by_dimension just extends an existing gap to a new, more prominent view.

## User impact
Any user who customizes their board (reassigns a model's role, adds a capability-based or custom-model seat, or has ever changed board membership over time) sees dashboard review-dimension health that is silently wrong or incomplete -- a model's calls appear under the wrong lens, or vanish from the breakdown entirely, and the vast majority of historical calls get retroactively re-labeled every time the board config changes, so past performance/security/quality trends are not trustworthy for anyone who has ever changed their board.

## Cost of inaction
The Stats view's by-dimension breakdown (and the pre-existing Models and roles / Errors tab views that share the same underlying helper) keep silently misrepresenting review-dimension health for any user with a customized board, and historical dimension stats keep getting silently rewritten every time the board config changes, with no indication to the user that this is happening.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The dashboard's board-derived views (the new Stats by-dimension breakdown, the existing Models and roles tab, and the Errors tab fallback hint) resolve the review lens for a call using the user's actual effective board -- the built-in default board, OR a per-repo board: override in config.yaml when one is set -- instead of always hard-coding the built-in default board.
- [ ] A model whose role was reassigned by a custom board: entry, or a model that only exists in a custom board and not in the built-in default, shows up under its real, configured lens in these views instead of the wrong lens or not at all.
- [ ] The historical-attribution question is resolved one way or the other on purpose: either the lens is snapshotted per call at the time it ran (mirroring how brainstorm persona roles are already recorded per call), so old calls keep showing the lens that was true when they ran even after the board config later changes -- or, if that is judged too costly for now, the dashboard UI explicitly labels the breakdown as reflecting today's board shape, not history.

title: Dashboard Models tab shows junk rows from malformed -m input and leaked test logs
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Investigated the review-cli dashboard's Models and Roles tab against Alex's real log history (134 thousand plus log files). Found two independent, confirmed-live root causes for junk rows. First, the CLI's model-selection flag accepts any string with no shape validation, so a caller who passes a prompt or message as that flag by mistake gets the free text spliced verbatim into the supposedly redacted log header, and the dashboard's model attribution regex then grabs just the first word of that leaked text and mints a permanent junk row (examples seen in real logs: oc:and, oc:the, oc:whether, oc:question-mark). Second, the streaming-backend test file drives the real log-writing code path directly in about ten test functions without isolating the log directory environment variable, so it falls back to the real OS-standard log directory - confirmed with a live timestamp during this investigation, meaning every unguarded test run has been polluting the real dashboard with synthetic fake-prefixed rows (over six thousand files found).

## User impact
The real dashboard Models and Roles tab is unusable for its stated purpose of seeing real board-seat health at a glance - about 89 rows in current output, most of them single-character or dictionary-word garbage or test-only synthetic backend names, drowning out the ten real board seats.

## Cost of inaction
The Models tab keeps accumulating unbounded junk rows on every test run and every future flag mistake, getting less readable over time, and the log header's redaction guarantee stays silently violated for any oversized free-text value passed to that flag.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] review diff -m 'free text with spaces' (also quorum, just-ask, sessions resume, qa) exits non-zero with an actionable error instead of silently dispatching the text as a model
- [ ] running python -m pytest -q no longer writes any log file into the real OS-standard log directory (verified by running test_streaming.py's synthetic-backend tests and confirming zero new files land outside the isolated test temp dir)
- [ ] a dashboard call whose logged opencode/omp header is not the clean 'backend -m model' shape attributes to the bare backend name instead of minting a one-word junk model row such as oc:and
- [ ] the Models and Roles tab's Raw board health section defaults to board-seat rows only, with a toggle to reveal off-board/extra rows and a count of how many are hidden

## What


## Why (motivation)

title: Dashboard ok/error accounting undercounts paywall and empty-output calls as OK
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Codex flagged this during review of the Stats-view redesign (review-cli#343): reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py's has_error field is exit-code-authoritative, but classify_call() (used for the dashboard's own health badges) treats an exit-0 paywall or empty-output call as a real failure via is_paywall/has_real_content, independent of exit code. The new by_dimension breakdown reuses the SAME has_error-only split the pre-existing top-level ok_calls/error_calls counters already use, so this is a pre-existing, cross-cutting gap in the whole dashboard's success accounting, not something newly introduced by the Stats redesign -- but the new by-dimension view makes the gap more visible, which is why it surfaced now.

## User impact
When Alex looks at the dashboard to see which model or seat is healthy, a seat that is actually stuck (paywall-blocked, out of quota, or returning nothing every time) still shows up as passing, because those calls exit 0. He can't trust the success-rate numbers or the new per-dimension breakdown to tell him a seat is broken -- he'd have to notice it some other way first.

## Cost of inaction
The dashboard's headline success-rate numbers and the new per-dimension health breakdown keep silently over-crediting paywall and empty-output calls as OK, understating real failure rates for exactly the failure modes review-cli's own classifier was built to catch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] compute_stats() and any view derived from it (the top-level ok_calls/error_calls/success_rate cards, and the Stats view's by-dimension breakdown) classify a completed call as OK only when classify_call() returns HEALTH_OK, not merely when has_error is false -- so an exit-0 paywall call (Fable returns exit 0 with an unavailable body) or an exit-0 empty/no-real-content call is counted as a failure, matching what classify_call() already reports elsewhere in the dashboard (the health badges, the Models and roles tab).
- [ ] A regression test covers at least one exit-0 paywall call and confirms it is counted as a failure (not OK) in both the top-level success rate and the by-dimension breakdown.

title: review diff wedges at zero CPU before any reviewer starts, on large diffs
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Observed three times in one session against a repository with a large staged diff (5600 and then 5800 lines). Each time the process printed the diff statistics, then sat at 0.0% CPU with no child processes and no output file, until an external timeout killed it. Once it had run 16 minutes, once 15. The same command on a small diff completes in about four minutes. The machine was under heavy memory pressure in each case, which may be the trigger rather than the size.

## User impact
A caller can trust that review finishes or explains itself, instead of building a watchdog to tell a slow run from a dead one.

## Cost of inaction
Any automation calling review has to guess a timeout and re-run blind, and a wedge in a pre-commit gate looks exactly like a slow review.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A wedged run is detectable: review either makes progress, fails with a diagnosis, or exits — it does not sit at zero CPU indefinitely producing no output file
- [ ] The diff-review path has a bound of its own, so a caller does not have to wrap it in an external timeout to avoid waiting forever
- [ ] When it does give up, the output says where it stopped — resolving models, launching a reviewer, waiting on one — rather than leaving an empty log

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: no external entities referenced

comments.body:
Fourth occurrence, same session, and this one narrows it usefully.

The diff was **small** this time — about 200 lines across two files — which rules out diff size as the trigger. What the four have in common is a machine under heavy memory pressure (swap 90%+ of 16-20 GB). Elapsed at kill: 16 min, 15 min, 14 min. Each time: the process prints nothing, has no child processes, sits at 0.0% CPU, and writes no output file, until an external timeout or a kill ends it.

Two runs in between, on the same machine and the same day, completed normally in about four minutes — so it is intermittent rather than a hard block.

If it helps narrow further: the wedge is before any reviewer subprocess exists. `pgrep -P <pid>` returns nothing at all while it is stuck, so whatever it is waiting on, it is waiting alone.
