title: review-cli: make harness, provider, model, effort, and review mode compose independently instead of tangled seat strings
body:
## What
Today a board seat is one opaque string (e.g. codex:gpt-6-astra, oc:zai glm-5.2) that bakes together which harness runs it (claude-code CLI, codex CLI, opencode CLI, or an HTTP gateway like commandcode, zai, gemini, or openrouter), which provider/model it calls, and only when a preset is chosen, what reasoning-effort level it uses. Harness selection is entirely inferred by matching string prefixes in resolve_backend (in reviewlib backends.py) -- there is no structured field that says this seat runs through the codex CLI. Effort level is already a real, independent field on the board reviewer record, settable per-provider via an --effort flag in any review mode, but preset selection (the curated multi-seat board bundle) only exists for the diff review mode, and each preset hardcodes one fixed effort level for every seat in it rather than expressing this set of models times this effort level as two independently swappable choices. Quorum, brainstorm, and just-ask modes have no preset concept at all -- they only take a flat model list plus the same global effort override. Proposal: (1) add an explicit harness field to the seat representation, parsed once at config-load time via the existing prefix table instead of re-inferred at dispatch time, with an unrecognized prefix failing loudly instead of silently falling through to the opencode catch-all; (2) keep effort as the existing independent axis but make preset definitions reference it explicitly as model-set times effort-level, two named independently overridable choices, instead of one baked tuple; (3) extend the preset concept to quorum, brainstorm, and just-ask so all four review modes can select the same named combinations; (4) make model aliases (e.g. an alias that resolves to the claude harness, another that resolves to the codex harness) show their resolved harness in the board-display output.

## Why (motivation)
Harness, provider, model, effort, and review mode were added incrementally as ad-hoc string prefixes plus a bolted-on effort field. There is no single place that answers what actually runs when you pick a model without reading the string-prefix-matching logic, and preset bundles -- the main lever for review strength -- only exist for one of the four review modes.

## User impact
Engineers configuring or debugging which model backend actually reviewed their code have to trace string-prefix matching logic instead of reading an explicit field. This makes it easy to misconfigure a review board (for example, believing a friendly alias runs one harness when it silently routes to another) and blocks giving quorum, brainstorm, and just-ask the same preset-strength selection that diff review already has.

## Cost of inaction
The seat-string tangle keeps growing with every new harness or provider added; each addition risks colliding with an existing alias or silently falling through to the opencode catch-all. The CTO's specific ask -- independently picking harness, provider, model, and effort per review mode -- stays unimplementable without an even larger rewrite once more ad-hoc prefixes accumulate.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A short design note documents the target seat/harness/effort/preset data model before implementation starts
- [ ] The backend-resolution function raises or warns instead of silently defaulting to opencode for an unrecognized seat prefix
- [ ] The board-display output prints the resolved harness for every seat, including aliased ones
- [ ] At least one of quorum, brainstorm, or just-ask can select a named model-set plus effort combination equivalent to a diff-review preset, without needing a full board
- [ ] Existing seat strings keep working unchanged; no board config in the wild breaks

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: slash-separated tokens are code identifiers (seat strings, file paths, mode names) not repo links

comments.body:
Alex clarified the target design more precisely today (2026-09-05), verbatim intent, worth pinning exactly so it doesn't drift from this ticket's own proposal (1), which is subtly different (that proposal makes harness an EXPLICIT field a role/seat still specifies; Alex's actual ask is that a role/seat should specify ONLY a model, with harness and provider resolved automatically underneath — never required as user-facing input at all):

- "надо чтобы харнесы, провайдеры, модели, эффорты, режимы review сквозным образом ортогонально работали" — harness, provider, model, effort, and review mode should compose orthogonally end to end.
- "нужно прописывать в ролях модели а не харнесы, харнес и провайдер должны подбираться автоматически" — a role's config should name a MODEL, never a harness-prefixed string; harness and provider selection is the system's job, not something the role definition should ever need to spell out.

Concretely, this means: today's `codex:gpt-6-astra` / `oc:zai/glm-5.2` seat-string shape bakes the harness choice into the very thing a role config writes down. The corrected target is closer to a role saying just `gpt-6-astra` or `glm-5.2`, with a separate resolution layer deciding "this model routes through the codex CLI" / "this model routes through opencode" — the same way a person doesn't pick which car factory line manufactured their car, they just pick the car. Proposal (1) in this ticket's body (an explicit `harness` field) is a real improvement over today's implicit string-prefix matching, but if it still requires a role/preset author to WRITE a harness value at all, it falls short of what Alex is actually asking for — the harness field should be something `resolve_backend`/the model registry DERIVES from the model name (a single canonical mapping of model -> harness+provider, maintained once, not re-specified per role), not something every seat/role config carries explicitly.

This doesn't change this ticket's priority (still the largest, most foundational item in review-cli's harness-parity work, appropriately last in the dispatch order per the earlier gap-catalog research) — just recording the precise target shape now so the eventual implementer doesn't have to re-derive it from a chat transcript.

title: review-cli: add named preset tiers so commit-time review runs medium and PR-time review runs large
body:
## What
The CTO wants commit-time review (the fast local pre-commit loop) to run at a medium strength tier and PR-time review (the heavier pre-merge gate) to run at a large tier. Today the preset dictionary only defines three tiers -- default, heavy, and light -- and the default tier is light (about to change again via an already-open pull request, see below). The names medium and large do not exist as preset names today (medium currently only exists as an unrelated effort-level value, not a preset name). Also, contrary to an assumption that a PR-time call site already exists, there is none: review-cli's own commit-hook script tells the developer to run review diff with a staged flag and a task code, with no explicit preset flag at all, so it falls through to whatever the default preset happens to be. Neither review-cli's own CI nor the sibling rig-cli repo's CI or ship scripts invoke a diff review or quorum review as an automated PR gate today -- PR-time review is currently a manual, agent-driven practice, not a wired CI step. This ticket also flags a sequencing dependency: an already-open pull request (branch fix/rounds-default-brainstorm-grounding-preset-light) changes the default preset from default to light and touches the same pool-guard messaging and board-sizing text that a new preset tier would also need to touch -- this ticket's work should land after that pull request merges, or be rebased onto it, to avoid a preventable merge conflict on the same lines.

## Why (motivation)
The CTO wants a deliberate two-tier strength policy -- fast and cheap for the frequent commit-time loop, thorough and expensive for the once-per-PR merge gate -- instead of every call site silently inheriting whatever the default preset happens to be, which today is not tied to commit-vs-PR context at all.

## User impact
Without named tiers, commit-time and PR-time review keep running the same undifferentiated default strength: either every commit pays the cost of a heavy PR-grade review, or pull requests get reviewed at the same light effort as a quick commit-time check.

## Cost of inaction
The PR-time gate stays a manual, un-differentiated review call with no strength guarantee, and any future automation that wires review-cli into CI as a PR-time gate will pick an arbitrary preset instead of the intended large tier, repeating the same ad-hoc-default problem this ticket is meant to close.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The preset dictionary gains two additional named tiers, medium and large (either as literal new entries, or the commit-hook and any future PR-gate call explicitly pass the existing light tier labeled medium in docs/hook text, and the existing heavy tier labeled large -- pick one approach and document why)
- [ ] The commit-hook install command's printed instructions include the explicit medium-tier preset flag in the review-diff command it recommends
- [ ] A PR-time review invocation, wherever the orchestrator ends up wiring one, explicitly passes the large-tier preset instead of an implicit default
- [ ] This ticket's changes land after the already-open preset-default pull request is merged, or the branch is explicitly rebased onto it, verified by a clean merge with no conflicts on the preset dictionary or pool-guard message strings
- [ ] Requesting the board for both the medium and large presets both print a valid board

## What
The worktree review-cli-wt-fable-disable (intended branch fix/fable-100pct-failure) is parked in a detached HEAD state mid an interactive rebase, halted on an unresolved conflict in the changelog file, untouched for roughly 8 days as of 2026-09-05. It cannot be resumed, finished, or safely removed without first deciding whether to abort the rebase (discard it, return to the branch tip) or manually resolve the conflict and continue.

## Why (motivation)
A worktree stuck mid-rebase for over a week blocks that branch's fix from progressing and risks being forgotten entirely, unlike a merely-uncommitted worktree which at least has recoverable, inspectable state.

## User impact

title: review dashboard stop/disable report success while an ad-hoc run instance on the same port stays alive
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex relayed a direct complaint from another agent: it ran review dashboard disable, review-cli printed a stopped confirmation, but the dashboard process (started earlier with the ad-hoc run form) was still alive and still holding the memory. Traced the cause in [reviewlib/cli.py's own docstring](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/cli.py) for the dashboard subcommand dispatcher: run is explicitly a separate, unmanaged ad-hoc path with no pidfile, so stop/disable (which only knows about the pidfile-tracked managed instance) has no way to see it, yet reports success as if it always fully controls the port.

## User impact
Alex or an agent trying to free up memory or restart the dashboard runs stop or disable, believes the port and process are now clear from a confident success message, and moves on — while the real process silently keeps running and holding memory, which is exactly the kind of leaked background process this whole investigation is trying to eliminate.

## Cost of inaction
Every future memory or port-conflict investigation on this machine re-discovers the same false confidence from stop/disable and has to manually hunt for the real PID by hand, the same way this one did.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] After starting the dashboard with the ad-hoc review dashboard run --port <N> and separately with the managed review dashboard start, running review dashboard stop or review dashboard disable warns explicitly that a process is still listening on the dashboard's port when it did not start that process, instead of printing an unqualified stopped/success line. — forced: Verified live: with a real process listening on the dashboard's actual default port (7878), 'review dashboard disable' now prints 'dashboard: autostart disabled, but something is still listening on 127.0.0.1:7878 (pid 82914) — it was not stopped by this command' and exits 4, instead of the old unqualified success. CLI-only behavioral change, no visual UI to screenshot.
- [x] A new test reproduces the exact scenario a real user hit: an ad-hoc run process bound to the default port, then stop/disable called against the same port, asserting the output names the still-alive PID/port rather than claiming success. — forced: Confirmed in agent-tools#538 (merged): python3 -m pytest tests/test_agenttools_service.py -q — 118 passed, including a dedicated regression test reproducing the exact ad-hoc-run-then-disable scenario from this ticket.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- screenshots: CLI/behavioral change, no UI

comments.body:
Fixed upstream in the shared \`agenttools_service\` lib (the bug applies equally to config-web, tg-ctl, and any future consumer, not just review-cli's own dashboard command) — see [agent-tools#538](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/538), merged. \`ServiceManager\` gained a real \`probe_port()\` (TCP connect on both loopback families + best-effort PID lookup); \`stop\`/\`disable\` now probe after acting and report an explicit warning + exit 4 when something is still listening, instead of an unqualified success.

Independently verified live, not just trusting the PR description: with a real process listening on the dashboard's actual default port (7878), \`review dashboard disable\` now correctly prints \`dashboard: autostart disabled, but something is still listening on 127.0.0.1:7878 (pid <real-pid>) — it was not stopped by this command\` and exits 4, matching both acceptance criteria exactly. title: review diff --staged --commit refuses with "staged diff changed" on a byte-identical index after a CLEAN review
body:
## What
In the conloca/landing repo (main checkout /Users/ultra/work/conloca-landing and its agent worktrees), running `review diff --staged -C . --task "#138" --commit -m "claude:claude-opus-4-8"` on 2026-09-05 and 2026-09-06 completed the review with a CLEAN verdict and then refused to create the checkpoint commit with a "staged diff changed" error. The staged index was byte-identical before and after the review (verified with `git diff --cached | sha256sum` on both sides of the run, and by re-running the same command twice in a row with no edits in between). A plain `git commit` issued immediately afterwards, against the same index, succeeded and passed every pre-commit hook, including the review-before-commit gate. Three independent agents hit this on three different branches: [conloca/landing PR 109](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/109), [PR 130](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/130) and [PR 139](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/139) (task code was [issue 138](https://github.com/conloca/landing/issues/138)). Workaround used every time: run `review diff --staged` without `--commit`, then `git commit`. No gate was bypassed and no `--no-verify` was used. This is distinct from [review-cli 208](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/208), [209](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/209), [216](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/216) and [381](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/381): those concern the pre-commit hook hash tolerance and the diff.noprefix mismatch; here the hook is not involved at all, the refusal comes from the `--commit` checkpoint path itself after its own review passed.

## Why (motivation)
The atomic review-then-commit path is the documented safe way to satisfy the review-before-commit gate, and it silently fell back to "review passed, nothing committed" on three separate PRs in one weekend. Each time an agent had to notice the missing commit, re-run the review or commit by hand, and re-wait the ship dwell timer.

## User impact
Anyone using `--commit` as intended ends up with a passed review and no commit, and either loses the review stamp on the next restage or commits manually and wonders whether the gate was actually satisfied. It cost several hours of agent time across the three conloca/landing PRs linked above on 2026-09-05/06.

## Cost of inaction
The `--commit` flag stays unreliable, so every caller learns to avoid it and the atomic review-plus-checkpoint guarantee it exists to provide is lost; the false refusal also looks like a security gate firing, which trains people to reach for bypasses.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With an unchanged staged index, `review diff --staged --commit` creates the checkpoint commit after a CLEAN review instead of refusing with "staged diff changed"; reproduced on a real repo, not only under mocks
- [ ] A regression test snapshots the staged-diff hash before dispatching the review, re-reads it after, and asserts the checkpoint proceeds when the two match; it fails on the current code path that produced the false refusal
- [ ] When `--commit` does refuse, the error names the two hashes it compared and the diff serialization it used, so the next occurrence can be diagnosed without re-running the review

title: Task-code key is sensitive to a leading "#": iterations recorded under 105 are invisible to gh ship, which reads "#105"
body:
## What
The review-cli iteration store keys recorded reviews by the exact task-code string passed to `--task`. `review diff --task 105` and `review diff --task "#105"` therefore write to two different keys. The gh ship review-quorum gate (agent-tools ci/ship/ship.sh, which calls `review task CODE --check`) derives the code from the commit or PR trailer, so it always looks up the `#105` spelling, exactly as written in "Closes #105". Every iteration an agent recorded with the bare number is invisible to the gate. Observed on 2026-09-05 and 2026-09-06 in the conloca/landing repo: after real multi-model reviews had run under `--task 105`, `--task 125` and `--task 129`, `gh ship` reported the quorum as 0/3 for [PR 109](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/109), [PR 130](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/130) and [PR 131](https://github.com/conloca/landing/pull/131), and several agents re-ran the full review round under the `#`-prefixed spelling to compensate. No gate was bypassed. This is separate from [review-cli 213](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/213) and [217](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/217), which bind iterations to repo and diff identity; the mismatch here is purely the spelling of the key.

## Why (motivation)
The review-quorum gate exists to prove a diff was actually reviewed before merge; when the proof is filed under a key the gate never reads, the gate blocks correct work and the only visible symptom is "0/3 iterations" after reviews visibly ran. Three PRs in one weekend paid for full duplicate review rounds because of the spelling of a flag value.

## User impact
Whoever runs `review diff --task 105` (the natural spelling when the number comes from a ticket ID) gets a review that counts for nothing at ship time, then has to guess why quorum is empty, re-run every seat under the other spelling, and wait out the dwell timer again. On the three conloca/landing PRs above this was several hours of agent time and model spend on 2026-09-05/06.

## Cost of inaction
Every new agent or human rediscovers the split key by losing a review round; the wasted spend recurs on every repo that uses gh ship, and the quorum store keeps accumulating orphaned records under bare-number keys that nothing will ever read.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] The task code is normalised to one canonical form at both write time (`review diff --task`) and read time (`review task CODE --check`), so `--task 105` and `--task "#105"` land in and read from the same record; or, if the bare-number form is rejected, the rejection names the expected spelling and exits non-zero before any model is dispatched — forced: CLI/store-keying behavior, no UI to screenshot (matches ticket's own skipped-gates note). Proof: reviewlib/stats.py normalizes both write-time (record_run) and read-time (quorum_check/iterations_for_task) task codes via the same _github_issue_twin/dual-key aliasing so '105' and '#105' resolve to one merged record set. Verified by tests/test_run_stats.py::test_quorum_check_bare_digits_visible_under_hash_prefix_review_cli_389 and test_quorum_check_hash_prefix_visible_under_bare_digits_review_cli_389 (both PASS, see /tmp/389_proof_tests.log) -- each records under one spelling and reads back successfully under the other.
- [x] A test records iterations under one spelling and checks the quorum under the other, for both directions, and passes only when the lookup finds them — forced: Same non-UI CLI behavior as criterion 1. Proof: the two tests cited above (bare_digits_visible_under_hash_prefix / hash_prefix_visible_under_bare_digits) are exactly 'records under one spelling, checks under the other, for both directions' -- both PASS (/tmp/389_proof_tests.log, lines 5-6).
- [x] The `review task CODE --check` and gh ship refusal output list the exact key they searched and any near-miss keys found in the store (same digits, different prefix), so a mismatch is diagnosable from the refusal alone — forced: Non-UI CLI stderr text output, no screenshot applicable. Proof: reviewlib/cli.py's _quorum_check_subcommand prints '[review task] note: searched key ... found ... in the store (same digits, different #)' on a failed/empty check whenever a same-digits twin key exists, in BOTH text and --json modes. Verified live and via tests: test_quorum_check_near_miss_keys_on_failed_check_review_cli_389, test_cli_check_near_miss_key_note_text_mode_review_cli_389 (text mode), test_cli_check_json_near_miss_fields_* (json mode), plus PR #431's follow-up fix (near_miss_counted/near_miss_ever_passed) ensuring the note's claim is accurate, not just present -- all 14 relevant tests PASS, see /tmp/389_proof_tests.log.

title: review diff: say WHY there is no diff (clean working tree) and how to review a committed branch
body:
## What
reviewlib/modes/review.py prints 'No diff to review.' (exit 1) whenever the working-tree diff is empty. review diff only reads the working tree (or --staged, or a piped diff); it never diffs a branch against its base. An agent that has just committed sees an empty diff and reads the message as a tool failure: on 2026-09-06 two agents in one day concluded that a DIFFERENT review binary was on PATH in a background shell (there is only one, ~/.local/bin/review and ~/.files/bin/review both symlink /Users/ultra/xp/review-cli/bin/review) when the real cause was a clean tree plus a background shell whose cwd had been reset. ## Why (motivation)
The bare 'No diff to review.' cost two agent investigations in one day (agent-tools#565 follow-up), both chasing a phantom duplicate binary.

## User impact
An agent or a person who just committed gets told what to run instead of guessing at PATH problems.

Every post-commit review attempt keeps failing with a message that points at nothing, and the next agent repeats the same wrong diagnosis.

title: codex review seat can run commands outside its read-only sandbox (created and closed rig-cli#384 during a review)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
On 2026-09-07 07:20Z a codex seat of a review of https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/372 ran task new / task check --force / task done and created+closed https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/384 while the review is documented as read-only. title: opencode/omp backend seats inherit parent stdin, can hang forever misdiagnosed as quota-exhaustion stall
body:
## What
reviewlib/process.py's _run_streamed (the shared subprocess runner every backend uses) Popens with stdin=subprocess.PIPE if input_text is not None else None. review_opencode and review_omp in reviewlib/backends.py both pass the whole prompt as argv and never pass input_text, so for these two backends stdin is left as None -- the child (opencode/omp CLI) INHERITS whatever fd the review-cli python process itself has as stdin, instead of getting a closed/empty stdin. If that inherited fd is a pipe/tty that never reaches EOF (e.g. review dispatched as a background job by an orchestrating agent whose own stdin is an open, non-closing pipe), and the opencode/omp CLI tries to read stdin at all (a common CLI pattern: read piped stdin when not a TTY), the child blocks indefinitely at 0% CPU with zero output. Observed live 2026-09-07 ~21:33 UTC: review diff --staged --task 389 spawned an opencode run subprocess that was sampled hung in a stdin-read syscall, 0% CPU, no output, and had to be manually killed and relaunched with stdin explicitly redirected from /dev/null to make progress. codex/claude backends are unaffected because they always pass input_text (stdin=PIPE, fed then closed). This is very likely the actual root cause behind the 'opencode/oc:zai stalls with zero output' class already band-aided by the true-silence stall watchdog and cooldown mechanism -- that mechanism detects the symptom (zero output) and cools the seat down as though the provider's quota were exhausted, when the real cause can be review-cli's own subprocess wiring inheriting a bad stdin, unrelated to the model or provider at all.

## Why (motivation)
review-cli routinely runs as a subprocess of a background/detached orchestrating agent whose own stdin is not guaranteed to be closed or EOF-terminated; the shared subprocess runner must never let a child backend inherit that fd

## User impact
A user who kicks off a code review sees it hang forever on one model seat for no visible reason, then that seat gets silently disabled for everyone's later reviews on the mistaken belief its quota ran out -- even though it was healthy the whole time

## Cost of inaction
Every review invocation whose parent process has a non-EOF stdin risks an indefinite opencode/omp hang, and the existing stall-watchdog keeps misdiagnosing it as provider quota exhaustion, cooling down seats that are actually fine

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Reproduce the hang: spawn review_opencode (or review_omp) with the process's own stdin connected to an open pipe with no writer/EOF and confirm the opencode/omp child blocks with zero output before the fix — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof428/1_prefix_hang.txt)
- [x] _run_streamed's Popen call passes stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL (never None/inherited) whenever input_text is None, so an argv-only backend call can never read the parent's stdin — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof428/2_devnull_source.txt)
- [x] Regression test asserts the Popen stdin kwarg is DEVNULL (not None) for the input_text=None path, and existing input_text-provided paths (codex/claude) keep stdin=PIPE unchanged — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof428/3_regression_test.txt)
- [x] With the fix, the same reproduction (open non-EOF pipe as parent stdin) no longer hangs: the opencode/omp child completes normally, provably unaffected by parent stdin state — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof428/4_postfix_nohang.txt)

title: review diff --pool 0 with an all-same-role config roster silently skips role padding, breaking gh ship's quorum floor
body:
## What
reviewlib/cli.py's --pool 0 seat-count warning (added under review-cli#309, ~lines 5038-5063) fires only when a config models:/board: roster has FEWER seats than SHIP_MIN_ROLES -- it never checks role DIVERSITY. A roster with 3+ seats that all share the same role (e.g. 4 seats all role=correctness) sails through with no warning under --pool 0. Separately, the role-repair call ensure_min_distinct_roles (~line 5450) is gated on effective_pool_size > 1, but --pool 0 sets effective_pool_size = 0 (~line 4970) and nothing later raises it back up before the repair check runs, since the roster already exceeds SHIP_MIN_ROLES in raw seat COUNT (so the short-roster/single-model pad paths never apply either). Net effect: the board dispatches with only 1 distinct role despite having several seats, and review task CODE --check / gh ship fails later with no diagnostic pointing back to the actual cause (a same-role config roster combined with --pool 0).

## Why (motivation)
review-cli#309 fixed role padding for the light-preset, single-model, and short-roster cases, but --pool 0 combined with an all-same-role config roster is a distinct shape that path never covered -- it is the one remaining way a recorded review can still silently fail the self-merge-authority gate's role-diversity requirement

## User impact
Someone running review diff --task CODE --pool 0 against a config roster where every seat happens to share the same role gets no warning, then hits an unexplained gh ship / review task --check failure later with nothing in the earlier run's output pointing back to why

## Cost of inaction
The role-diversity blind spot review-cli#309 was filed to close remains open for this one specific combination, and whoever hits it has to rediscover the cause from scratch the way review-cli#309 itself had to be rediscovered

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] review diff --task CODE --pool 0 against a config roster whose seats all share one role warns the same way the existing seat-count --pool 0 warning already does for a too-few-seats roster, naming the role-diversity problem specifically — proof: ![proof](/tmp/433-ac-proof.txt)
- [x] ensure_min_distinct_roles's role-repair actually runs for a --pool 0 dispatch when the roster's raw seat count is high enough to skip the short-roster pad but its role diversity is still below the ship floor, so the real dispatch does not silently drop to 1 distinct role — proof: ![proof](/tmp/433-ac-proof.txt)
- [x] A regression test drives a 4-seat, single-role config roster through review diff --task CODE --pool 0 and asserts the resulting recorded dispatch has at least SHIP_MIN_ROLES distinct roles (or, if that is genuinely unachievable from a same-role roster, asserts a clear warning/failure instead of a silent 1-role dispatch) — proof: ![proof](/tmp/433-ac-proof.txt)

title: throttle review pool by live harness 5h/7d limits
body:
## What
reviewlib usage_limits.py is the existing throttle and it is tg-ctl-only. load_snapshot (usage_limits.py lines 92-120) reads the tg-ctl usage-latest.json files under ~/.config/tg-cli and never calls harness limits. DEFAULT_LIMIT_THRESHOLD = 70.0 (usage_limits.py line 53) excludes near-limit seats then reuses another model. When every reachable seat is over that threshold, select_pool_with_reuse in reviewlib config.py still spawns the least-depleted via _least_depleted_index (config.py lines 799-809 and 883-885) — including a 100 percent exhausted account. REVIEW_MAX_CONCURRENCY in reviewlib process.py is a memory semaphore, not quota. Family map today: prefixes claude: and codex: plus exact codex. _RATE_LIMIT_NAMES = 5-hour and weekly (usage_limits.py line 48) identified by English labels, not window_seconds.

Evidence from current code:

usage_limits.py lines 5-13: "tg-cli's tg-ctl daemon... persists the latest sample... This module reads that SAME file as a best-effort, READ-ONLY signal" — no harness path exists.

config.py lines 830-833: "candidates = under_limit if non-empty; otherwise (every reachable seat is near its limit) the SINGLE seat with the lowest usage percentage ... so the board never goes empty just because every seat is somewhat depleted."

config.py lines 883-885 call _least_depleted_index on every reachable seat and keep that one candidate even at 100 percent.

Origin: Alex ask 003 / ThrottlePool. Cost: an exhausted 5-hour window still pays for real claude and codex dispatches until the provider 429s.

Desired: prefer live JSON from `harness limits --all --json` (harness-cli 0.5.0 at https://github.com/alex-mextner/harness-cli) as the usage source; keep tg-ctl as fallback for families harness did not report. Identify 5-hour and 7-day windows by window_seconds (18000 and 604800), not English labels. Refuse spawn when that family's more-restrictive 5-hour or 7-day window is used_percent >= 100. Do not invent a fake max-7 concurrent-agent cap. Do not edit harness-cli. Work lives in https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli.

## Why (motivation)
When Claude's 5-hour window is used up, review still launches those seats and burns the account. The pool's least-depleted fallback will pick a 100 percent exhausted family rather than skip it, so a doomed dispatch runs until the provider 429s.

## User impact
When you run a code review after Claude's 5-hour session quota is already at 100 percent, review-cli still starts those Claude seats. You wait on a dispatch that cannot succeed, the provider eventually rejects it, and the run has already spent time (and any leftover quota) on a doomed call instead of skipping that family and using a seat that still has budget.

## Cost of inaction
Exhausted 5-hour and 7-day windows keep paying for real claude and codex dispatches until the provider 429s. The board will even pick a 100-percent-used account as the least-depleted fallback rather than shrink the pool, so every review after the window fills burns the account again.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] When harness Session window_seconds=18000 is at 100%, allow_spawn_for_model("claude:claude-opus-4-8") is False and usage_percent_for_model is 100 — proven by unit test test_harness_session_100_refuses_claude_spawn in tests/test_usage_limits.py — proof: ![proof](tests/test_usage_limits.py::test_harness_session_100_refuses_claude_spawn)
- [x] Weekly 7-day at 88% and Session 20% yields percent 88 (max of windows) and spawn is still allowed — proven by unit test test_harness_weekly_max_still_allows_spawn in tests/test_usage_limits.py — proof: ![proof](tests/test_usage_limits.py::test_harness_weekly_max_still_allows_spawn)
- [x] A missing or unusable harness card fails open (spawn allowed), matching missing tg-ctl — proven by unit test test_harness_missing_card_fails_open in tests/test_usage_limits.py — proof: ![proof](tests/test_usage_limits.py::test_harness_missing_card_fails_open)
- [x] 5-hour and 7-day windows are identified by window_seconds even when the English name is unexpected — proven by unit test test_harness_identifies_windows_by_seconds_not_name in tests/test_usage_limits.py — proof: ![proof](tests/test_usage_limits.py::test_harness_identifies_windows_by_seconds_not_name)

title: Pad default panel --task when only one live engine is reachable
body:
## What
What is concretely wrong: reviewlib/cli.py task_role_pad (around line 5408) is gated on len(explicit_models)==1. After merged https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/436 (commit c4cc41f on origin/main) and the earlier -m one-model pad in https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/433, an explicit `-m grok --task` pads that engine across SHIP_MIN_ROLES. A recorded panel with NO -m still does not: when only one DEFAULT_MODELS engine is reachable, just-ask, quorum, and brainstorm --task record 1 role.

Evidence (captured at ticket time from origin/main c4cc41f):
```
task_role_pad = (
    bool(task_code)
    and mode.name in ("review", "just-ask", "quorum", "brainstorm")
    and len(explicit_models) == 1
    and effective_pool_size > 1
)
```
Panel pad source is board_from_models(explicit_models, config), which is empty when -m is omitted. Existing test test_cli_panel_task_one_model_pads_to_ship_min_roles only covers the -m path.

Where this came from: HatchBrainstorm remaining gap after https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/436; gh ship hatches a recorded one-engine default panel because review task CODE --check needs 3 distinct roles.

Pseudocode: after models resolve, also set task_role_pad when panel_mode and not explicit_models and len({default_distinct_key(m) for m in models})==1; pad via ensure_min_distinct_roles(board_from_models(explicit_models or list(models), config), pad_min). Keep len(explicit_models)==1. Keep effective_pool_size > 1. Do not pad without --task.

## Why (motivation)
A recorded just-ask, quorum, or brainstorm --task is supposed to satisfy the ship floor. The -m one-model pad already exists; the default (no -m) path with one reachable engine is the hole that still hatches gh ship.

## User impact
When you record a panel review with --task and do not pass -m, and only one review engine is actually available (for example only Grok), the run stores a single role. Later, gh ship / `review task CODE --check` refuse to merge because they need three distinct reviewer roles. You cannot ship the work even though you did run a recorded review — the tool silently under-counted roles instead of asking the one live engine once per role.

## Cost of inaction
Every recorded default-panel --task on a one-engine day keeps hatching gh ship. Agents re-run reviews or invent extra -m flags; merges stall. The -m pad in https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/436 does not cover the common no-flag path.

title: Stop dashboard hot path scaling with the 154k-file log corpus
body:
## What
What is concretely wrong: after https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/426 merged, reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py `_scan_log_dir_entries` (parser.py:1436) still os.scandir()s every name in the log dir on every fingerprint/SSE poll, and `load_sessions` (parser.py:1132) still Path.iterdir + is_file + get_or_parse over EVERY artifact. `_log_dir_fingerprint` (server.py:136) holds `_SessionCache` lock on every `/api/runs` `/api/stats` request while that scan runs. Evidence measured 2026-09-08 against ~/Library/Logs/review-cli: 154328 entries (147619 .log, 6705 .md); os.scandir only 0.702s; `_scan_log_dir_entries` 6h window 1.849s (4634 windowed, total_count 154333); /api/health 2.018s contended then 0.16s/0.02s; GET http://127.0.0.1:7878/api/runs?gap=90 HUNG (never returned). Origin: ask 064; parent ticket https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/151 still OPEN; closed review-cli#425 was intake noise. Follow-ups https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/155 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/156 are out of scope. Fix shape: (A) directory-mtime-gated name-list cache in `_scan_log_dir_entries` — reuse names when os.stat(log_dir).st_mtime unchanged, still .stat() the windowed subset (live-streaming invariant; APFS append does not bump parent dir mtime). No TTL debounce. (B) Bound `load_sessions` default parse to last 7 days via filename-stamp window matching `review stat --days`, reusing the stamp-prefix + min(newest_valid_stamp, now) directory-relative anchor so 2026-06 fixtures stay inside the window; days<=0 = all history; wire ?days= on /api/runs and /api/stats.

## Why (motivation)
PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/426 only skipped .stat() for old files. The hot path still pays O(total historical file count) for every name listing and for every full parse. https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/151 remains open because the dashboard is still unusable on this machine's real 154k-file log corpus.

## User impact
When you open the review dashboard in a browser, the Runs list stays stuck on Loading because /api/runs never returns. You cannot see recent reviews, stats, or live activity. This is not a visual glitch — the page is empty until the request finishes, and on a long-lived install it does not finish. Closing the tab and reopening does not help; every page load hits the same full-corpus scan under a lock.

## Cost of inaction
The live dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:7878 stays hung on /api/runs as the log corpus keeps growing (already 154k files). Every SSE poll and every fingerprint under the session-cache lock keeps scanning all names, so latency gets worse over time, not better. The board is unusable for day-to-day review of recent runs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Second `_scan_log_dir_entries` on an unchanged dir where only an in-window file grew: os.scandir call count stays 1, but the scan sees the new size/mtime (count calls, do not time). Proof: pytest test_scan_log_dir_entries_reuses_name_list_when_dir_mtime_unchanged.
- [ ] Creating a new matching file forces a rescan and total_count moves. Proof: pytest test_scan_log_dir_entries_rescans_when_a_new_file_is_created.
- [ ] `load_sessions` on thousands of old stamped files plus a handful of recent ones returns only the recent-window sessions and only parses/opens those; days=0 returns all. Proof: pytest test_load_sessions_default_window_skips_old_stamped_files.
- [ ] Existing review-cli#151 windowing tests stay green: test_scan_log_dir_entries_stat_count_bounded_by_window_not_total_corpus, test_scan_log_dir_entries_observes_a_live_streaming_file_growing, test_log_dir_fingerprint_and_snapshot_logs_share_the_bounded_scan. Proof: the same pytest -k filter.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- screenshots: No UI change; this is a latency fix. The broken state is /api/runs hanging (never returns), which has no meaningful screenshot.

title: Walk ROLE_FALLBACK_MODELS before different-role reserve
body:
## What
ROLE_FALLBACK_MODELS is listing-only after https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/449 (ticket https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/445). Mid-run failover in reviewlib/panel.py run_board_with_failover (around line 609) does reserve_queue.pop(0) with the next-priority seat's OWN role. A Grok/security quota fail therefore promotes DeepSeek/tests instead of staying on security (Qwen then glm-5.2). Startup select_pool and split_pool_reserve skip an unavailable seat and pull the next different-role board seat rather than substituting the role's fallback (Sol down should keep a consistency seat via Astra).

Evidence captured on origin/main f82ff42 (walk-role-fallbacks worktree) with _FakeBackends: pool equals GROK_SEAT security, reserve equals DeepSeek tests, Grok rc=1:
  dispatched: oc:xai/grok-4.6 then oc:commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
  usable_models: oc:commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
  usable_roles: tests
  stderr: [review-cli] board: Grok [security] failed — promoting reserve DeepSeek [tests] (oc:commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro)
The security fallback list is Qwen3.7-Max, grok-4.6, glm-5.2. DeepSeek must not be promoted while that list has a remaining unused model.

Follow-up to listing-only https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/449 — do not reopen that PR. Walk ROLE_FALLBACK_MODELS on seat exhaustion/error BEFORE the next-priority (possibly different-role) reserve. Custom seats whose model is not on the role list still fall through to reserve.

Pseudocode: cand = next_role_fallback(failed, used_models=used); if cand: next_round.append(cand)  # role-fallback, do not pop reserve; else: reserve_queue.pop(0).

## Why (motivation)
https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/449 published per-role fallback lists but the dispatcher still pops the next-priority reserve. With Grok quota thin, a security seat fail currently ships a tests-lens DeepSeek verdict instead of Qwen or GLM security. Listing-only leaves the published lists decorative.

## User impact
When you run a board review and Grok (security) is out of quota, the replacement review should still be a security review (Qwen, then GLM). Today you get DeepSeek reviewing tests instead, so a security hole can ship because the backfill looked at the wrong lens. Same for Sol being down at start: you should still get a consistency review from Astra, not lose that lens.

## Cost of inaction
Every Grok quota miss silently swaps security coverage for a tests reviewer. Security findings that Qwen or GLM would have caught are never asked. The lists on --show-board keep claiming fallbacks that dispatch never uses, so operators trust coverage they do not have.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Failed GROK_SEAT security is replaced by the next unused security fallback (Qwen agentic seat, then zai glm-5.2), not DeepSeek/tests, while that role list still has a remaining model. title: smoke.py _smoke_env() breaks pytest import for spawned subprocess tests on local user-site-packages installs
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
_smoke_env() (tests/smoke.py lines 73-82) redirects HOME to a fresh temp dir for every subprocess it spawns (line 77: "HOME": home). On a machine where pytest is installed to the per-user site-packages directory (e.g. ~/Library/Python/3.14/lib/python/site-packages, resolved from $HOME) rather than a venv, any subprocess launched with this env can no longer resolve 'import pytest' because Python's user-site lookup now points at the empty temp HOME instead of the real one. Confirmed while shipping https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/458 (MiMo 2.5 board seat): running the full smoke suite (tests/smoke.py::test_reviewlib_unit_files, which spawns tests/test_effort_run_flag.py as a subprocess) failed with 'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named pytest', unrelated to the PR's diff (git diff --cached tests/smoke.py touched only unrelated lines). Root-caused live: python3 -c 'import pytest' succeeds directly (from /Users/ultra/Library/Python/3.14/lib/python/site-packages/pytest/__init__.py), confirming HOME redirection, not a missing install, is the cause. Does not reproduce on GitHub Actions CI, which uses a normal venv where pytest sits on sys.path independent of HOME. Full repro transcript: history://MimoSeatFinish.ShipMimoSeat (search for _smoke_env).

## User impact
Anyone running the local smoke suite on a machine with a per-user pytest install (common for contributors not using a venv) hits a confusing, unrelated-looking ModuleNotFoundError that has nothing to do with their actual change, wasting time chasing a false regression signal.

## Cost of inaction
Contributors keep hitting and re-diagnosing this same false-positive failure on every local smoke run on affected machines, and it will keep getting misattributed to unrelated PRs the way it nearly was for https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/458.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] 1. _smoke_env() either preserves a usable site-packages path for spawned subprocesses (e.g. by copying/symlinking the real user-site pytest into the redirected HOME's expected location, or by setting PYTHONPATH/pytest explicitly) so that a subprocess test which itself imports pytest succeeds on a machine using a local (non-venv) user-site pytest install.
- [ ] 2. OR the smoke suite explicitly detects this local-only failure mode (missing pytest importable from the redirected HOME) and skips/xfails the affected subprocess test with a clear, actionable message, instead of letting a raw ModuleNotFoundError surface as an opaque failure.
- [ ] 3. Verified locally on a machine with pytest installed via user site-packages (not a venv): re-running the previously-failing subprocess test (e.g. tests/test_effort_run_flag.py invoked as a subprocess by test_reviewlib_unit_files) no longer raises ModuleNotFoundError, and CI (which already passes) remains green.

body:
## What
This isn't claiming review-cli is fundamentally broken -- the actual root cause of today's failures was ordinary quota/credit exhaustion on several seats under heavy concurrent load, which is expected and not a bug by itself. The real problem is that review-cli gave no clear signal that THAT was what was happening: every failure looked the same (an opaque fail_count), so from the outside there was no way to tell 'quota ran out, this is expected, wait or reduce load' apart from 'something is actually broken.' See --why for the concrete evidence.

## Why (motivation)
Dug into the actual per-call logs under ~/Library/Logs/review-cli/ for the exact failure window (2026-09-08T23:43Z to 2026-09-09T06:27Z) to find the real root causes, not just the aggregate fail_count. Found THREE distinct, precisely-identifiable causes, all already present in the per-call log text but none surfaced anywhere aggregate (run-stats.jsonl only has fail_count, no reason):
(1) GLM (both the z.ai and commandcode routes, since they share the same underlying zai-org account) hit a genuine, clearly-worded quota exhaustion: {"error":{"code":"1310","message":"Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted. Your limit will reset at 2026-09-10 21:15:09"}}. This is real and correctly a 429 -- not a bug in itself, just needs to be classified and surfaced.
(2) Grok hit genuine, clearly-worded credit exhaustion: "personal-team-blocked:spending-limit: You have run out of credits or need a Grok subscription." Also real, also should just be classified and surfaced, not a bug in itself.
(3) One GLM attempt (20260909T045232_027313Z-GLM__security_-retry-0001.log) failed with a completely different, NON-quota error: "Unexpected error / database is locked" -- this is review-cli's OWN local SQLite database hitting lock contention, almost certainly because of the heavy concurrent load (many subagents calling review diff in parallel against the same machine/config). This is a real review-cli bug, not a provider limit, and is the kind of database/cache concurrency safety gap already tracked by https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/319 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/339.
(4) Opus stopped being attempted entirely after 2026-09-08T23:43:23Z with an opaque {"name":"UnknownError","data":{"message":"Unexpected server error. Check server logs for details.","ref":"err_7ea41b69"}} -- this one is genuinely NOT classifiable from the message alone, which is exactly the 'unknown error, just show it plainly' case Alex asked for -- it should have been surfaced verbatim in whatever output/report the calling agent saw, instead of collapsing into the same undifferentiated failure as everything else.
Net finding: about 2/3 of today's reserve-pool failures really were mundane, already-clearly-worded quota/credit exhaustion (points 1-2) that should simply have been classified and reported as such (not treated as review-cli being broken) -- but a real, distinct review-cli concurrency bug (point 3) and a genuinely opaque unclassified error (point 4) were mixed in and indistinguishable from the quota cases without reading raw per-call logs by hand.

## User impact
Anyone running review diff -- a solo developer, or a fleet of many parallel agents each independently using it as their pre-merge quality gate -- silently loses automated code review entirely for hours whenever the top seats are busy, with no clear signal that the fallback itself is broken versus just slower. Today this meant roughly a dozen pull requests across a large fleet merged on manual review plus a secondary check instead of the intended multi-model board, for several hours, without warning.

## Cost of inaction
The reserve pool stays decorative rather than functional: every time the primary seats are saturated -- exactly when a reserve pool matters most, and an increasingly normal usage pattern for this tool -- review diff will keep silently degrading to zero real reviews for the duration, and the unpaid-providers exclusion will keep leaking a provider it is specifically configured to skip, quietly burning whatever credit or rate-limit budget that provider has left.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When the top-priority seats (Opus, Codex) are unavailable under heavy concurrent usage, the reserve pool that review diff falls back to actually succeeds at a reasonable rate instead of failing every single attempt
- [ ] The commandcode zai-org GLM seat is never dispatched when config.yaml or the REVIEW_UNPAID_PROVIDERS env var lists it under unpaid_providers -- confirmed today it still got dispatched and counted in run-stats.jsonl despite this repo's own config.yaml listing it there
- [ ] The actual per-seat failure reason (auth error, credits, rate limit, or something else) is visible in run-stats.jsonl or a companion log during a reserve-pool-only window, not just an aggregate fail_count -- related to https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/277 's visibility gap but specifically about reserve-pool seats during a top-seat outage, not the shortfall notice itself
- [ ] When a seat's failure is a RECOGNIZED error type (rate limit, quota/credits exhausted, auth failure, transient network error, etc.), review diff reports that specific classification clearly (not just an opaque fail_count) and, where appropriate, signals that the seat should be retried later rather than treated as a hard failure
- [ ] When a seat's failure is an UNRECOGNIZED error type (doesn't match any known classification), review diff surfaces the raw error text plainly in its output at completion, instead of swallowing it into an undifferentiated fail_count
- [ ] The 1310/'Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted' and 'spending-limit'/out-of-credits patterns are recognized and classified as quota-exhausted (not a generic failure) in whatever output the calling agent/session sees, mirroring what the per-call logs already contain
- [ ] A 'database is locked' failure (review-cli's own local sqlite contention under concurrent invocation) is classified distinctly from a provider-side quota/credit error, since it needs a different fix (retry-with-backoff or WAL mode on review-cli's own db) not a 'wait for quota reset'

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- Relates to #277: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/277
- Relates to #301: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/301
- Relates to #339: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/339
- Relates to #319: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/319

title: omp/claude multi-account seats: log carries no account/credential identity
body:
## What
Add account identity to the per-call log for a multi-account omp/claude seat, sourced from omp's own usage_history table (correlated by call time) or from omp's own CLI output if it ever surfaces the chosen account.

## Why (motivation)
omp's agent.db (~/.omp/agent/agent.db) tracks multiple distinct accounts per provider (e.g. 3 separate anthropic accounts, per usage_history's account_key/email columns), and omp itself decides which account serves a given call. review_omp (reviewlib/backends.py:1156-1265) passes only --model to the omp CLI and never records or queries which account omp internally picked.

## User impact
An operator debugging a failing or rate-limited account cannot tell from review-cli's own logs which of several configured accounts served a given call -- only the model/provider. They must manually cross-reference omp's agent.db by timestamp to find the account, which is slow and error-prone during an incident.

## Cost of inaction
Multi-account incident diagnosis stays a manual sqlite query against omp's private db instead of a grep over review-cli's own logs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A per-call log for an omp/claude seat that used one of several configured accounts records that account's identifying label in its header or a dedicated line.
- [ ] The account identity is sourced from omp's real usage_history table, correlated by call start and end time -- not guessed or hardcoded.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: hyphenated field-name phrases (account_key, email fields) false-positive as repo/path references; no actual repo/path link intended

title: ~/Library/Logs/review-cli/.call-log-cache.pkl is 6.4GB of orphaned dead weight
body:
## What
Delete the orphaned ~/Library/Logs/review-cli/.call-log-cache.pkl file (6,856,831,944 bytes, mtime Aug 30) once confirmed dead. This is a one-time manual disk cleanup, not a code change -- review-cli's shipped code never reads or writes this filename today, so there is nothing to script into a startup cleanup routine without inventing unneeded scope.

## Why (motivation)
git log --oneline --all -- reviewlib/dashboard/call_log_cache.py shows only two commits (https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/324 introduced the persistent cache, https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/336 capped its memory). call_log_cache.py's own module docstring states a single pickle-the-whole-cache blob was tried first and rejected in an earlier review round, in favor of the current per-file SQLite/JSON design. A repo-wide search for pkl or pickle usage under reviewlib finds zero live code paths that read or write a .pkl file -- only that historical docstring mention of the rejected design.

## User impact
Anyone running review-cli's dashboard or review stat on this machine is silently sitting on a Library/Logs directory that is 6.4GB heavier than it needs to be, with two similarly-named multi-gigabyte cache files next to each other and no way to tell by looking which one is actually used -- wasting their disk space and, if they go investigate, their time.

## Cost of inaction
The 6.4GB stays wasted indefinitely, and the ambiguity keeps costing investigation time for anyone who notices the two cache files.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Confirm no code, including tests, opens or references .call-log-cache.pkl by exact filename anywhere in the repo (already checked: zero hits outside one historical docstring mention).
- [ ] The file is deleted from disk by a human operator after that confirmation.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: opencode stall-retry loop writes no retry-log entry between its up-to-3 attempts
body:
## What
Have each non-final stall attempt inside _run_opencode_with_stall_retry call write_retry_log with a stall-specific kind, attempt number, and max attempts, mirroring how the outer retry layer already records its own events.

## Why (motivation)
_run_opencode_with_stall_retry (reviewlib/backends.py) retries a stalled zai/glm opencode call up to 3 times, but unlike the outer in-seat retry layer (reviewlib/retry.py, which calls write_retry_log for every retry, seat-fatal, and promote event), this inner stall-retry loop never calls write_retry_log between attempts -- only the terminal record_cooldown call marks that repeated attempts happened at all, and that state lives in a cache file, not a human-readable log. Each of the up-to-3 attempts writes its own ordinary per-call log via _run_streamed, indistinguishable from 3 unrelated single-shot calls.

## User impact
Someone reviewing a run's logs after a stalled model call sees three separate, ordinary-looking log files for the same model within a few minutes of each other with nothing tying them together -- they have to notice the pattern themselves and guess it was a stall retry, instead of finding one clear record that says so.

## Cost of inaction
Diagnosing a stalled opencode seat stays a manual pattern-matching exercise across multiple unlabeled log files instead of reading one explicit retry record, the same way every other retry path in this codebase already works.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the first N-1 stall attempts inside _run_opencode_with_stall_retry writes a retry-log entry recording the model, attempt number, and max attempts.
- [ ] A stalled-then-recovered call (attempt 2 succeeds) still leaves attempt 1's stall visible in a retry log, not just the final success.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: 'in-memory/cache-file' is a plain descriptive phrase, not a repo/path reference

title: Per-call logs can be left with no closing EXIT footer when review's process is killed externally
body:
## What
Extend the live-children registry to also carry each backend child's own log file path, and have kill_live_children best-effort append a short KILLED marker line to each live child's log before sending SIGKILL, for the caught-signal and internal-backstop paths.

## Why (motivation)
Real sample logs confirm calls where the log has only a header line plus [stderr] Working... and nothing else -- no TIMEOUT marker, no EXIT line (examples: 20260803T114533_181094Z-omp-r0.log, 20260814T005939_052244Z-omp-r0.log, 20260821T102928_144429Z-omp-r0.log, all 88 bytes). reviewlib/process.py's own comment block near its heartbeat-interval constant documents this exact failure mode from a real 2026-09-07 incident (a review diff killed by hand after 40+ minutes of silence) and says the root cause could not be pinned down because per-call logs from that window were abandoned mid-write with no closing footer at all. Root cause: kill_live_children (process.py) is called from both the internal backstop and install_signal_reaper's signal handler, and it only stores each live child as a bare (proc, pgid) pair -- it has no reference to that child's own log file path, so even the one code path that could inject a closing marker before the process dies has nothing to write it to.

## User impact
When someone kills a hung review diff by hand or lets an internal safety timer do it, every log file that was still open at that moment looks identical to a call that is still silently running -- there is no way to tell after the fact which log was the actual multi-minute hang everyone is trying to diagnose.

## Cost of inaction
The exact incident review-cli's own code comments describe (2026-09-07: root cause of a 40+ minute hang could not be pinned to a specific call) keeps recurring, with each recurrence costing investigation time that a single closing marker line would have saved.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A backend call killed via a caught interrupt signal leaves its per-call log with an explicit KILLED marker instead of ending mid-stream with no footer.
- [ ] The fix note explicitly states it cannot help against an uncatchable kill signal of review-cli's own process -- that remains an OS-level limit, not something this change claims to close.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: SIGTERM/SIGINT/backstop is a plain descriptive phrase naming signal types and a module concept, not a repo/path reference

title: review diff: hard-unavailable board seats vanish with no log record
body:
## What
Add a write_skip_log primitive to reviewlib/process.py following the same 0600, best-effort, per-event-file sidecar convention as write_retry_log, and call it from modes/review.py's board dispatch path once per seat that ends up in neither the pool nor the reserve, passing the existing human-readable unavailability reason.

## Why (motivation)
config.py's select_pool_and_reserve_with_reuse explicitly drops any board seat that fails its availability check from BOTH the dispatch pool and the mid-run reserve -- its own docstring says an unavailable seat is in neither list. Because no backend function is ever invoked for a seat in that state, none of the normal per-call log paths ever run either, so a hard-unavailable seat (no key, no CLI, an active cooldown, an exhausted provider chain) leaves no trace anywhere on disk. This is confirmed distinct from the already-correct unpaid-provider path: unpaid_provider_result is called from inside each backend function and does write a sidecar log today (real proof: a 268-byte omp log recording that a provider is marked unpaid/disabled and the seat is being skipped, exit 1) -- but that only fires for calls that reach inside a backend function; a plain no-key or cooldown seat never gets that far.

## User impact
An operator running review diff against a configured multi-seat board, where some seats are down for any reason, sees only that fewer seats ran than expected -- with zero durable record anywhere of which seats were skipped or why, unless they happen to separately run the board-status display at that same moment, which can already disagree by the time it is checked.

## Cost of inaction
Debugging a degraded review board stays guesswork: the operator has to reconstruct which seats were unavailable and why from memory or by re-running a separate status check, instead of reading it straight out of the run's own logs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A hard-unavailable board seat produces a skip-log file under the review log directory containing its model and unavailability reason.
- [ ] A seat that IS selected into the pool or reserve produces no skip-log entry.
- [ ] Existing board-dispatch tests pass unmodified.

## Screenshots
(none)

- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: kimi-code/k3 is a model identifier from the reviewer board, not a repo/path reference

title: Capacity check: distinguish confirmed quota exhaustion from cooldowns, unknown health and unusable routes
body:
## Outcome
`review capacity-check [--preset NAME] [--json]` provides accurate, account/route-scoped evidence for the active review configuration. A consumer can recognize a genuine all-candidates quota outage without interpreting missing data or unrelated failures as permission to skip review.

## Why / user impact
The original request is to stop repeated manual escalation for the same confirmed fleet-capacity outage. Incorrect affirmative evidence would instead allow review gates to be skipped when the real cause is a local bug, unknown health or a healthy alternative account that was not examined.

## Parent, specification and consumer
Parent: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/492
Specification: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/docs/ecosystem-grooming-2026-09-10/docs/specs/2026-09-10-review-contracts.md#review-runtime
Consumer task: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/705
Inventory/health producer: https://github.com/alex-mextner/harness-cli/issues/26
Implementation candidate, not merged: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/473

## Verified grooming findings — 2026-09-10
PR #473 is OPEN at 6be25c8a54b8a7091fc4e0eb0e58ac38e1c80bdd. The named capacity_check.py is absent from the default branch at inspection. Inspect/reuse this PR rather than creating a duplicate implementation.

Source: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/6be25c8a54b8a7091fc4e0eb0e58ac38e1c80bdd/reviewlib/capacity_check.py
1. `seat_exhaustion_evidence` accepts ANY active cooldown, without classifying its reason as quota exhaustion or binding it to the actual account/route.
2. `board_capacity_report` places candidates with NO exhaustion evidence into `available`, even when their health is unknown.
3. `checked_at` timestamps report creation; it does not establish freshness of each underlying observation.

An isolated execution of the copied functions with stubbed dependencies confirmed: two cooldowns whose reason is `local database is locked; quota unknown` produce `all_exhausted: true`; no evidence produces both candidates under `available`. This is a copied-function contract probe, not the repository suite, a live-provider test or proof that every fixture reason occurs in production.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Emit a versioned result with evaluated configuration/preset identity, candidate route/account identities, coverage, underlying observation times and typed reasons.
- [ ] `all_exhausted=true` requires a NONEMPTY candidate set and applicable, fresh affirmative quota evidence for every eligible candidate, including eligible account/role fallbacks. Unknown, stale, unsupported, unmapped or failed collection makes the assertion false.
- [ ] A cooldown is counted as quota evidence only when its structured, applicable cause proves quota exhaustion. Local database errors, authentication failures, network errors and generic silent/stalled calls remain distinct causes; they do not become quota merely because a cooldown exists.
- [ ] Known usable, exhausted, unavailable for other reasons and unknown candidates are separate. Do not label lack of exhaustion proof as confirmed availability.
- [ ] Preserve account specificity: one exhausted account cannot gate a healthy distinct account, and shared quota identity is represented explicitly rather than inferred from a provider label.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the two verified function cases above, zero candidates, mixed accounts, stale observations, malformed results, missing source and account fallbacks.
- [ ] Run a producer/consumer contract test with agent-tools#705 proving incomplete evidence does not authorize an exception and unrelated CI/protection gates remain unchanged.
- [ ] Document CLI/JSON compatibility, the exact evidence predicate, source limitations and a durable test result at the accepted revision.

## Priority / closure
P1. Not blocked on completing the entity TUI or a wholesale adapter rewrite: introduce the contract using available sources plus explicit unknowns. This task and agent-tools#705 unblock review-cli#476 only when their actual outcomes are verified; Alex's separate implementation-approval gate on #476 remains intact.

title: review diff hangs indefinitely: wire true_silence_timeout into review_codex, review_claude_cli, and review_omp's _run_streamed calls
body:
## What
reviewlib/backends.py's review_codex, review_claude_cli, and review_omp (_review_omp_once) call reviewlib/process.py's _run_streamed WITHOUT the true_silence_timeout kwarg, unlike review_opencode which already has it wired (reviewlib/model_behavior.py's true_silence_timeout_seconds(model), ~5min default). A subprocess on any of those 3 backends that produces literally ZERO bytes of output (observed live: mimo via omp, 13-30+ min, 0% CPU, zero output) falls back to the generic ~20min idle floor instead of being reaped in minutes. This ticket adds the missing true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model) kwarg to those 3 call sites, plus a backend-agnostic regression test proving _run_streamed itself reaps a zero-output subprocess quickly when the kwarg is set. It intentionally does NOT add the _record_true_silence_if_needed cooldown-recording extension for these backends - that is tracked separately by https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/235's second acceptance criterion - narrower scope, timeout wiring only.

## Why (motivation)
Reported live: 'review diff' hangs 13-30+ minutes with 0% CPU and zero output regardless of model picked, including -m mimo alone. mimo routes through omp (config.py's MIMO_SEAT), and review_omp's _run_streamed call has no true_silence_timeout, so a genuinely stuck or never-talking omp child pays the full ~20min idle floor instead of the ~5min true-silence cutoff review_opencode already enjoys. review_codex and review_claude_cli have the identical gap. See https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/235 for the full 5-call-site tracking issue this narrows.

## User impact
Any user running 'review diff' on a codex, claude-cli, or omp-routed model (including mimo) that goes truly silent waits up to ~20 minutes for a hung seat to be reaped, instead of the ~5min true-silence cutoff, with the harness appearing completely frozen (0% CPU, zero output) in the meantime.

## Cost of inaction
review diff keeps intermittently appearing to hang for up to 20 minutes on any of these 3 backends whenever the underlying model or CLI goes truly silent - the exact bug already reported live - even though the fix mechanism (true_silence_timeout) already exists and works, proven by review_opencode's existing wiring.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] review_codex's _run_streamed call passes true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model), landed either directly in this ticket's commit or via review-cli's concurrent omp-claude-fallback PR (noted explicitly in this ticket if so) — proof: ![proof](reviewlib/backends.py L388 (review_codex): true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model) passed to _run_streamed call at L380-392. Confirmed on origin/fix-omp-mimo-hang-timeout tip f1df8c4. Cross-referenced by tests/test_true_silence_backend_wiring.py::test_review_codex_passes_true_silence_timeout.)
- [x] review_claude_cli's _run_streamed call passes true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model), landed either directly in this ticket's commit or via the concurrent PR (noted explicitly in this ticket if so) — proof: ![proof](reviewlib/backends.py L3534 (review_claude_cli): true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model) passed to _run_streamed call at L3525-3535. Confirmed on origin/fix-omp-mimo-hang-timeout tip f1df8c4. Cross-referenced by tests/test_true_silence_backend_wiring.py::test_review_claude_cli_passes_true_silence_timeout and test_review_claude_cli_with_images_passes_true_silence_timeout.)
- [x] review_omp's _review_omp_once's _run_streamed call passes true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model), landed either directly in this ticket's commit or via the concurrent PR (noted explicitly in this ticket if so) — proof: ![proof](reviewlib/backends.py L1279 (inside review_omp, the _run_streamed call at L1270-1280 that dispatches _review_omp_once's subprocess): true_silence_timeout=true_silence_timeout_seconds(model) passed. Confirmed on origin/fix-omp-mimo-hang-timeout tip f1df8c4 (commit e6fe8c7 dropped a duplicate kwarg from an earlier merge, leaving exactly one correct true_silence_timeout= kwarg). Cross-referenced by tests/test_true_silence_backend_wiring.py::test_review_omp_passes_true_silence_timeout.)
- [x] tests/test_true_silence_hang_regression.py: a new backend-agnostic test calls reviewlib.process._run_streamed directly with a real zero-output-producing subprocess (sleeps, writes nothing), a short true_silence_timeout, and a generous timeout and idle_floor, and asserts it returns within seconds with returncode==125 and true_silenced is True - passes when run via python -m pytest tests/test_true_silence_hang_regression.py -v — proof: ![proof](New file tests/test_true_silence_hang_regression.py added (did not exist anywhere: not on main, not on this branch previously, not on any other open/merged PR including #477 omp-claude-fallback). Backend-agnostic: calls reviewlib.process._run_streamed directly with a real subprocess ([sys.executable, -c, 'import time; time.sleep(120)']) producing zero stdout/stderr, true_silence_timeout=1, timeout=60, idle_floor=60. Asserts returncode==125 and true_silenced is True and elapsed<20s. Registered in tests/smoke.py _UNIT_FILES (after test_true_silence_backend_wiring.py entry). Verified: python -m pytest tests/test_true_silence_hang_regression.py -v -> 1 passed in 1.23s (wall 1.6s), NOT the 120s sleep duration, proving the true-silence reap actually fires. Committed f1df8c454db56a1bf78e14fba9a8f1ef7fc8da52, pushed to origin/fix-omp-mimo-hang-timeout.)

## Screenshots
(none)

title: Adapter architecture: factual health, progress-aware liveness and fallback-first execution [design-gated]
body:
## Outcome
New harness/provider/model routes using existing capabilities can be declared without new special-case branches in the executor. Reviews use accurate route/account health and actual progress signals, try viable alternatives first, and terminate with an actionable reason once no permitted option remains.

## Why / original intent
Alex rejected simply adding the same timeout everywhere or moving one opencode-only constant. His clarification is explicit: try other model/provider/account combinations first; fail promptly when nothing can work; keep billing, limits and backend status accurate. Source clarification: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/476#issuecomment-5607861902.

## Parent / specification / existing decision
Parent: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/492
Specification: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/docs/ecosystem-grooming-2026-09-10/docs/specs/2026-09-10-review-contracts.md#review-runtime
Existing narrower ADR and its delivery remain credited: https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/490 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/d6594c279683dd57beae0959735ac44113404c85/.haft/decisions/476-backend-liveness-adapter-architecture.md.
The ADR compares extending ModelBehavior with a new BackendProfile. Keep the chosen small consolidation as a possible migration slice; do not pretend that moving a constant completes the universal architecture.

## Implementation gate — not satisfied by a document
- [ ] The capacity outcome is verified in https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/472 AND https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/705.
- [ ] Alex explicitly approves implementation of the reviewed architecture. Link the actual approval; a merged ADR or this grooming is not approval.
The previous checklist conflated a delivered decision record with this compound gate. Implementation stays blocked. No implementation PR should open under this task before both conditions are met.

## Architecture requirements
Separate protocol capabilities, route/account observations, declarative model behavior and generic execution policy. Reuse the existing process/cooldown/board machinery rather than adding a parallel engine. Account/provider discovery comes through the public harness contract: https://github.com/alex-mextner/harness-cli/issues/26.

## Acceptance criteria after approval
- [ ] Record alternatives, ownership, schema/versioning and a migration map from existing backend branches. Centralize genuinely per-model configuration without copying provider probes into review-cli.
- [ ] Keep authentication, billing, quota, connectivity, local-storage errors, process state and progress distinct, each with source/time/coverage. Unknown does not become authenticated or healthy.
- [ ] Every supported route uses the common liveness policy. Tests distinguish zero output, output followed by a stall, silent-but-evidenced progress, transport death and cancellation; silence/low CPU alone is not definitive remote failure.
- [ ] Fallback preserves requested role/effort and account scope, tries compatible plausible candidates without retry loops, and reports the terminal reason when alternatives are exhausted.
- [ ] Demonstrate config-only onboarding of a new route that uses an already implemented protocol/capability, with no new dispatcher/process special-case branch. A genuinely new protocol still requires an adapter; do not hide that engineering work behind the config-only claim.
- [ ] Retire the opencode shadow matcher/duplicated settings as part of the agreed migration, with existing behavior regression tests and an explicit compatibility policy.
- [ ] Producer/consumer conformance tests and a durable result at the accepted revision prove the architecture, not just a synthetic registry lookup.

## Existing work / exclusions
#474's narrow true-silence wiring is delivered and must not be redone. #486 tracks the separately reported worktree hang and its unconfirmed environment hypothesis. #479 covers account-selection correctness. The entity TUI (#487), capacity exception policy (#472/#705) and log migration (#480) remain separate tasks.

## Priority / closure
P1 architecture, DESIGN-GATED. Preserve the broad requested outcome while delivering approved increments. Do not close on the ADR, one renamed constant or a passing test that never exercises another route.
